In our research, we assess the effectiveness of recurrent neural networks that utilize data from Caenorhabditis elegans to predict neural activity. Specifically, we utilize information regarding sensory input, motor neuron interactions, and the nervous system topology to forecast motor neuron activity. By treating the prediction of future neural activity using past motor neuron behavior as a temporal regression task, we demonstrate that a recurrent neural network such as Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) can generate a model that outperforms baseline models. Additionally, we investigate which types of information are most crucial in predicting neural activity and find that including motor neuron past activity is the most critical factor. Our findings suggest that neural interactions play a significant role in information processing during Caenorhabditis elegans locomotion. The proposed methodology presents a novel approach to modeling the nervous system, which could have far-reaching implications for healthcare by contributing to the advancement of brain-prosthetic technology. Our results highlight the value of leveraging artificial neural networks in understanding the intricacies of biological systems and may inspire the development of future neurological restoration treatments. The source code for our experiment is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexander-pai/GRU_Celegans_Information_Projection.git. Additionally, our precomputed responses to your questions, along with 3D visualizations of the Caenorhabditis elegans nervous system and other related data, have been included in this abstract. An interactive HTML version of these results, which incorporates responses to your questions and allows for 3D exploration, can be accessed at https://github.com/alexander-pai/3D-Celegans-NN-Visualizations/. Our paper, which provides further explanation and context for these results, is available at https://www.mdpi.com/1999-4907/100/14/179/2020. The neuroprosthetic community may find the following related research (listed in reverse chronological order) to be of particular relevance. In particular: (1) our 2020 analysis (referenced in the abstract's conclusion), (2) our 2019 investigation of neural network-based models that relate motor neuron activity to motor neuron behavior, and (3) our earlier study comparing models that use information from Caenorhabditis elegans to predict motor neuron behavior. Effective regulation of neural activity is critical in various neurological and neuroprosthetic applications. Our paper presents a potential approach to modeling the nervous system and discussing the implications of our results for neurological restoration through neuroprosthetic technology

To arrive at this outcome, the authors establish the isomorphic connection between representations of the Zinbiel algebra and tensor products of linear transformations, leading to a characterization of the supersolubility in terms of a particular set of finite-dimensional linear transformations whose product falls within a specific subset. Additionally, the authors provide a straightforward condition ensuring the supersolubility of any given finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra. Furthermore, the characterization of finite-dimensional bilinear algebras with a solvable nilpotent representation is also established in this work. Ultimately, the authors conclude by identifying and illustrating all possible dimensions for a two-dimensional bilinear semigroup. Examples that demonstrate the conditions resulting from the main theorem are invalid are presented and examined. Additionally, a characterization of the solvability of a general colored Lie algebra in two dimensions is established in this work. To achieve these outcomes, the authors devise and present a range of original proofs, encompassing 6 distinct types, each characterized by their unique approach. The bulk of the proofs utilizes inductive arguments on the maximum length of decompositions. The global spread of infectious diseases is heavily influenced by the processes of migration and transmission. Migration significantly amplifies the potential for large epidemics, particularly in densely populated cities, by introducing infectious individuals into new areas, thus triggering massive outbreaks. Conversely, widespread migration can also impede the spread of infectious diseases on a large scale, essentially creating an urban barrier that slows the transmission of pathogens. Consequently, the relationship between migration and transmission is complex and highly variable, depending on a variety of factors including the scale of migration, population distribution, and the dynamics of disease transmission. While past research has explored the connection between migration and emerging infectious diseases, this study provides a comprehensive review of the relevant processes and their impact on transmission, focusing on populations that migrate internationally. It is well established that individual-level migration processes affect local and regional epidemiological outcomes, and that these migrations can be classified into four primary types, each involving distinct transmission impacts. The first type is urban migration that reduces national transmission rates, the second is targeted migration that maintains population aggregation, the third is dispersal that increases transmission by pushing pathogens into new areas, and the fourth is large-scale migration that can create an effective barrier against pathogens in certain geographic regions. Understanding these migration and transmission dynamics is essential for developing and implementing effective policies against emerging pathogens and mitigating infectious disease outbreaks. As global population trends indicate a shift towards urbanization, these migration and transmission dynamics will continue to evolve, underscoring the need for timely updates in population dynamics theories and applications. These population dynamics updates will have significant implications for various fields including public health, immigration policies, city planning, and infectious disease modeling, which have historically been based on outdated assumptions. The proposed framework aims to provide a practical solution, complementing the existing theoretical frameworks that largely overlook the role of migration in population dynamics. By exploring the complex relationships between migration and transmission, this study aims to inform migration and transmission policies, contributing to the advancement of infectious disease modeling and population dynamics. Exoplanetary systems with near-resonant orbital arrangements hold significant importance due to their rare occurrence and the insights they offer into early planetary system formation. Accurate verification of these systems' orbital patterns is crucial, as they have the potential to produce unique atmospheric and orbital changes. A recent study identified the near-resonant system K2-138, consisting of eight planets, with an orbital period ratio of approximately 3:2, but left the verification process incomplete. Our investigation sought to address this by addressing two key issues: incomplete data and systematic errors. We addressed these challenges through two approaches. Firstly, we utilized all available short-period transit data, doubling the number of data points. Secondly, we applied a novel method based on the Laplace resonant zones to eliminate incorrect solutions. Utilizing the DREUH near-infrared spectroscopy, we refined the analysis by incorporating anti-correlated noise. Our revised analysis confirmed the 3:2 resonance in the final seven planets, but failed to verify the resonance in the outermost planet. Analysis of Laplace resonant zones, Laplace indices, and phase-space curves confirmed the presence of the 3:2 resonance in the system, revealing a series of linearly overlapping epicycles that supported a resonant chain. Our results suggest that the resonance in the K2-138 system, consisting of seven planets, is a natural occurrence, likely the result of planet-planet interactions, and potentially preceded the loss of verifiability of the outermost planet's resonance. This study highlights the effectiveness of combining transit timing, orbital analysis, resonance validation, and phase-space curves to accurately identify resonant structures within planetary systems. Based on these findings, we propose that nearly resonant systems, such as K2-138, consist of planets that fail to verify the predicted resonance despite being part of a larger resonant chain. Further, we suggest that near-resonant systems may serve as intermediate formations between non-resonant configurations and precise resonant patterns, providing insights into early planetary evolution. Ultimately, we recommend that without verifiable confirmation, transit period third bodies should not be considered inevitable components of a resonant system. The associated data and code are available through the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/astroKIT/astroKIT/tree/main/papers/2023_0409. Additionally, we distribute an updated version of the fast, numerically-based transit timing algorithm utilizing the Kitsap-IT algorithm, available through https://github.com/astroKIT/astroKIT/tree/main/codes

The SiD Experiment at the Large Hadron Collider will utilize sensors based on an improved CMOS silicon technology to achieve precise energy and position measurement. This is done through advanced analog readout and precise timing, enabling the detection of long-range B meson decays. In the past, the SiD sensors underwent thorough characterization, revealing both promising and limiting features. Building upon this understanding, the report explores two potential modifications to the SiD sensor. The first involves enhancing charge collection by increasing the sensor thickness from 150 to 250 micron, despite potential issues with radiation hardness. The second modification aims to increase the sensor's gain through introduction of a gate structure, but this also comes with a potential gain uniformity problem. Both proposals are evaluated based on their detection capabilities and sensitivity in the detection of supersymmetric and extra-dimension signals, as well as in the study of the Higgs boson in hidden sector. The findings indicate that the initial sensor design shows sufficient measurement capacity for the study in question and the proposed modifications. Nevertheless, the increased thickness and introduction of the gate structure exhibit varying degrees of efficacy and require further study and testing in a real-world environment to determine their feasibility and applicability in the detection of these particles and processes. GP 2 is a dialect of guarded Horn clauses with a marked improvement in efficiency, particularly for scenarios involving numerous guards, due to a sound and accounted-for reduction to Horn clauses with data-dependent guards. This reduction leverages the properties of stratification to ensure the integrity of the interpretation, while also providing a syntactic condition that facilitates the detection and prevention of unacceptable guard rearrangements during program compilation. This paper presents a minor-step operational semantics for GP 2 that directly models its execution, without relying on the reduction to guarded Horn clauses with data-dependent guards. This semantics provides a useful comparison with other operational semantics and highlights the correctness of the reduction through a proof of equivalence between the two approaches. An analysis of the approach's potential extensions to cover non-terminating computations and finite partial ordering in the context of GP 2 semantics is also provided. Finally, a comparative study of GP 2 semantics and other related languages is offered. This study has significant practical implications, particularly when considering the integration of GP 2 with other programming languages that rely on partial orders. It demonstrates that GP 2 semantics can effectively guide the implementation of partial-order concurrency languages. The GP 2 project was previously published in 2011, this paper marks a 10-year anniversary of the work. The original GP 2 project was centered in China, this paper represents a collaborative effort between Chinese and Italian researchers. Despite GP 2 not gaining a significant following, the principles underlying the work have led to important influences in the field of logic programming and concurrency. A readable implementation of the GP 2 semantics, along with associated tools, is available for immediate use through the \gp2\ Java package. While this implementation was originally developed for testing purposes, its clarity and functionality are notable. A comprehensive testing framework, featuring both theoretical and practical tests, thoroughly validates the GP 2 semantics, providing a useful reference for research in logic programming and concurrency semantics. The material presented in this dissertation draws from the author's doctoral dissertation, which was defended at the University of Brescia in March 2022. This dissertation represents the first publication on the topic and is accompanied by two additional papers that build upon the content, specifically a publication in the journal Logic Programming and a forthcoming publication in the Journal Systems and Computational Science. Analyzing this data, researchers have developed an algorithm to identify potentially hazardous situations near these devices. A field test revealed that the algorithm provided accurate predictions in over 90% of cases. A key innovation involves categorizing locations as high, medium, or low risk based on the detected transient magnitude and the device's geographical position. Moreover, researchers have identified the most critical variables affecting performance and proposed strategies for improving the accuracy of failure predictions. This research aims to facilitate the implementation of more effective protection systems against lightning and other electrical discharges for the energy infrastructure. A software program, written in MATLAB, has been developed to analyze data from sensors and provide users with personalized risk assessments, which can be used to prioritize maintenance and ensure the energy infrastructure remains safe and resilient. Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) technology is expected to significantly contribute 
to reducing network congestion in millimeter wave (mmWave) networks by allowing 
interference. Nevertheless, managing interference remains a major challenge in 
mmWave networks. In an effort to overcome this issue, multi-group broadcast 
scheduling has been explored, but its high complexity in decoding requirements 
poses a major obstacle. This paper proposes a hybrid decoding approach, called 
Minimax Hybrid Decoding (MHD), designed to minimize decoding complexity for 
multi-group broadcast schedules. Firstly, an optimal schedule is obtained using 
a proposed matching-based algorithm. Next, users in each group are divided into 
two categories: primary and secondary groups. While users in the primary group 
are processed using standard layered linear precoders and decoders, those in 
the secondary group are processed using repacked sparse reception and zero-forcing 
transmission and low-complexity decoding. This division enables an efficient 
balance between precoding and decoding complexities. Numerical results show that 
MHD outperforms existing solutions in terms of sum-rate, complex decoding, and 
transmission performance, with a simple implementation in both high and low SNR 
conditions. This performance advantage is validated through various scenarios, 
including random user setups, random channel conditions, and urban outdoor 
environments. Furthermore, MHD is shown to be flexible and efficient in cases 
where user grouping may not be obvious. This paper offers insights into hybrid 
decoding for multi-group broadcast scheduling in mmWave networks and proposes a 
practical approach with a balanced performance of sum-rate, decoding complexity, 
and precoding efficiency. The proposed algorithm is expected to be a viable 
solution for autonomous scheduling in mmWave networks. Its performance can be 
leveraged as a benchmark for other algorithms in various scenarios. Analysis of 
HDD performance is expected to provide a standard for comparing existing and 
future algorithms in low SNR conditions. Additionally, considerations of HDD 
performance can be applied to other scheduling algorithms, including sum-rate or 
utility maximization. This research offers insights useful in designing and 
evaluating other algorithms in mmWave frequency-division multiple access 
scheduling. Considerations of precoding and decoding complexity, as well as zero 
data rate cases, may be applied to various other algorithms in this space. The 
decision-theoretic value of HDD performance can serve as a useful benchmark for 
evaluating other algorithms in mmWave networks. This work may be expanded to

Determining the masses of extremely neutron-rich atomic nuclei is crucial for understanding the intricate process of heavy element creation within cosmic supernovae explosions and for calculating the characteristics of essential elements involved in the r-process. However, these nuclei are temporarily stable at extremely high neutron densities found in the cores of these events. To address this, we utilized the AI-assisted machine learning approach for developing predictive models of nuclear weights based on theoretical predictions of nearby nuclei. This model excels in the heavily neutron-rich region, demonstrating a level of precision that meets current r-process investigations' demands. To validate our approach, we calculated the theoretical description of nuclear weights using a microscopic HFB theory with a constrained Hartree method. This comparison highlights minor discrepancies between our predictive model and the HFB approach, which remains within the predicted uncertainty range. To ensure the reliability of our results, we conducted a thorough analysis of our predictive model, taking into consideration the effects of nearby nuclei on the calculated weights. This study marks the first attempt to apply machine learning to the investigation of nuclear weights and will form the basis of future nuclear weight studies. Importantly, our model has significant implications for the understanding and interpretation of cosmic supernovae events, particularly in terms of their ability to investigate r-process events using the most precise and accurate methods available. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of machine learning applications in nuclear physics, particularly in regions that are difficult to investigate with existing theoretical models. Future developments in machine learning methods and integration with theoretical models will be essential for further improving our understanding of this heavily neutron-rich region. Additionally, our study highlights the possibility of applying this model to the investigation of various nuclear physics applications. Future investigations into the investigation of this region using experimental approaches such as SPESLI at ANL and other facilities will be critical for the development of this field. Future developments in experimental and theoretical investigations will be necessary for the interpretation and interpretation of our results. Superconducting devices used in quantum computing have a critical dependence on microwave dielectric quality, which we assess experimentally. We investigate this sensitivity by analyzing the dielectric loss of sapphire with extraordinary sensitivity, down to variations of less than one billion parts per billion, by measuring the phase shift of a superconducting qubit's frequency resonance across multiple scenarios: utilizing either a sapphire or a dilute calcium oxide substrate, in various configurations with or without an amorphous silicon buffer, at room temperature, and following an annealing process to eliminate defects. The data confirm that sapphire meets the stringent criteria for high-coherence superconducting devices, with the dielectric loss improving an astonishing ten trillion times following annealing to a level near the quantum limit, comparable to the best dilute calcium oxide performance. Additionally, adding an amorphous silicon buffer increases the dielectric loss by a factor of ten thousand, thus serving as an ineffective barrier. The research highlights the significance of ultra-high sensitivity in assessing microwave dielectric qualities and demonstrates a new method to quantify dielectric loss with unprecedented sensitivity, which could potentially broaden the applications of sapphire in quantum computing technology. Furthermore, this approach may offer insights for improving sapphire dielectric quality through substrate materials, processing optimization, and thermal treatment. Importantly, the methodology can be adapted for evaluating other microwave dielectric materials at the quantum limit, offering a promising pathway for identifying the most suitable materials to meet the rapidly increasing coherence demands of the quantum computing industry. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the feasibility of employing superconducting devices as ultra-sensitive experimental tools to investigate various aspects of physics, including solid-state materials research. Specifically, the research group has already leveraged this same sapphire substrate to discover a previously unknown stabilization effect known as the Bauerle stabilization, paving the way for the development of the first stable single-flip quantum gate, an essential technology to support the growth of the quantum computing revolution. Conversely, without the sapphire substrate's exceptional dielectric quality, the stabilization proved unfeasible. The study highlights the critical role of microwave dielectric quality in enabling novel quantum phenomena and gates, underscoring the significance of this aspect in the ongoing pursuit of large-scale quantum computing advancements. Moreover, the research suggests that the integration of sapphire and similar high-quality dielectric materials in superconducting quantum processors may provide a natural pathway to the so-called "superconducting quantum circuit crossbar," an emerging architecture poised to enable the development of a vast quantum information system capable of simulating complex systems or performing

In a material with all three indices of refraction having the same value, the optical pull phenomenon becomes singular and takes on an unusual form that needs reconsideration.  Specifically, when the material is not only isotropic but also invariant under inversion, the usual expression for optical pull becomes ambiguous and must be modified accordingly.  We demonstrate that by altering the expression, the case of uniaxial materials can be generalized to isotropic materials, and we explore the implications of this modification in the case of uniaxial materials with n1!= n2!= n3.  Our work also considers the particular example of a uniaxial half-space, where a mean-field approach to the expression for optical pull results in a surprising alignment of dipole moments with the optical axis.  We propose that this alignment phenomenon persists across various types of uniaxial materials and, more generally, that material isotropy implies this alignment in a solid under excitation.  Finally, we modify the expression for optical pull in materials that are isotropic but not invariant under inversion and discuss the resulting modifications in the cases of materials with n1!= n2!= n3 and n1 = n2 = n3.  (Source: arXiv:2202.11858 )

This framework consists of a template-driven visualization system, which allows users to create multiple visualizations in one image using various design templates. Each template creates an interactive focus area in the image, enabling users to switch between these focus areas to pinpoint and examine specific entities. This approach is enhanced by a summarization strategy that preserves key characteristics across different focus areas, thus allowing users to seamlessly transition and analyze various parts of the dataset. In recent times, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been extensively used in various domains such as social network analysis, drug design, and recommendation systems. This research investigates the transfer of knowledge within GNN architectures when applied to different industries and knowledge bases. We particularly evaluate the effectiveness of Inception GNN models, comparing their performance to other commonly employed GNN models. Our study is conducted on five diverse datasets, showcasing a methodical approach to analysing GNN architectures on multiple sources and knowledge domains. We also provide a step-by-step guide for researchers to reproduce the results, utilizing the PyGSP library on both GPU and CPU. Our study contributes significantly to the field of GNN architecture research by examining transfer learning in multi-loop GNN models and experimenting with varying network depths. Furthermore, we examine the impact of edge dimension on GNN performance. Our study's results reveal Inception GNN models outperform other models in most cases, but struggle on small datasets, whereas GraphSAGE models demonstrate superior performance on small datasets. Online community forums such as 'QA' and 'Recommendation' enable users to generate, collect, and disseminate knowledge, thereby serving as virtual knowledge bases for queries. The massive traffic on these platforms demands efficient access to relevant information, thereby prompting the development of various suggestion technologies. This paper presents an innovative dual feature distribution model (DDDM) that leverages users' diverse behavior and content to provide relevant suggestions. Specifically, the context of the question and the context of the answer are employed as the foundational elements for computing user-interest and question-relevance. By incorporating a dual memory mechanism that adapts to these contexts, the proposed DDDM model learns to accurately predict relevant suggestions. This paper outlines the underlying rationale, implementation details, and effectiveness of the proposed DDDM, showcasing its superiority through comparative evaluations on the Wikipedia, TencentYq, and Quora platforms. Furthermore, the paper describes an enhanced variant of DDDM, titled DDDM-E, which integrates additional content-producing features to provide more comprehensive suggestions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DDDM-E outperforms existing technologies and delivers suggested answers that are concisely articulated. DDDM-E is presently utilized in the real-world by Tencent's technology support team to provide user suggestions. Universal Learning, a project rooted in universal types and typed lambda calculus, has two primary objectives. Firstly, it seeks to simplify advanced machine learning concepts using fundamental mathematical constructs. Secondly, it aims to provide a common framework for diverse machine learning approaches, bridging the gap between theoretical foundations and practical applications. We introduce delta lenses, a key concept, as a means to represent learning transformations. We use delta lenses to describe and implement regularization, introducing lenses as a common framework that unifies various forms of regularization. We introduce delta lenses to describe learning transformations, our approach leads to a generalization of regularization that can be transmitted across various models, enabling a unified understanding of machine learning. We apply this transmission to CNNs, its adaptation to natural images, and discuss its potential applications in model averaging and reinforcement learning. 

Note: This research paper is a rewritten version of my PhD dissertation. Since the original work, significant advancements have been made in the field of delta lenses and universal transformation, especially in the transmission of transformations between types and values. We introduce two novel transmissions, one focusing on the relationship between sets and spaces, and another between algebras and domains. We also expand the transmission to dynamic delta lenses that incorporate explicit state changes, demonstrating its potential in the description of neural tangent kernels and showing a potential gap exists in the transmission to kernel-based methods, and discussing the implications of the findings for the explanation of the representation in the GPT-family models.

accurately predict a smooth wave speed when that speed increases with distance,
yet ucpu falls short in predicting smooth wave speeds that decrease with distance. 
Furthermore, ucpu tends to overestimate the minimum wave speed, leading to an
upper bound instead of the actual wave speed, a critical consideration in coastal
regions where ucpu predictions may not be adequate due to the effects of decreasing
wave speeds.  Consequently, ucpu should not be used in regions where this condition
holds true without further adjustments such as data rectification to account for ucpu's
limitations or the incorporation of higher-order terms to rectify this issue. 
Moreover, ucpu should be used with caution in coastal regions where ucpu's
predictions may lead to inaccuracies due to its failure to accurately predict wave
speeds in these areas.  Research into improving on ucpu should prioritize its logical

cpu(0) = 0.478 and ucpu(0) = 0.764 reveal that ucpu significantly overestimates
wave speeds, particularly near their actual minimum values.

This paper presents a detailed sequence of fibrations with stiff properties, focusing on precise transitions between these fibrations, which are key factors in both physical and mathematical contexts. Stiff fibrations have inherent connections with Legendrian knots, contact structures, and Hamiltonian dynamics, with precise sequences also playing a crucial role in encoding information about these topics via their fibrational structures. Our study provides a comprehensive analysis of precise sequences on Legendrian loops within a uniform closed polyhedron, showing that these sequences are highly constrained and cannot exist freely. We demonstrate that the only possible precise sequences occur between two specific types of stiff fibrations, namely, quasi-isomorphic and co-isomorphic stiff fibrations. Our findings have significant implications for the relationships between different forms of stiff fibrations and provide a foundational framework for our second main result, which involves the equivalence of different categories among stiff fibrations without sources or sinks. Our research ultimately reveals that co-isomorphic stiff fibrations are indeed equivalent, but this equivalence cannot be derived from quasi-isomorphic pairs, thus highlighting the unique nature of co-isomorphism in this context. Our work also addresses the open-ended question of whether precise sequences can arise from the transition between any two stiff fibrations, but interestingly, we find that this possibility does not exist. We demonstrate that any sequence of stiff fibrations must result in either quasi-isomorphism or co-isomorphism, thus resolving the question and shedding light on the precise sequences' inherent properties. The research provides a method for systematically calculating conservation laws and symmetries for various $n$-dimensional Ermakov systems. This approach enables the generation of TFS from various types of data, while also providing a method to assess the availability of the TFS for any given frame. This innovation employs a novel metric that calculates the similarity between frames, allowing the integration of temporal information and thereby enhancing the effectiveness of the routing system, which is particularly crucial in urban environments. The research also involves creating a dataset with annotated URLs from multiple web platforms to validate the proposed method. Experimental results on our dataset demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses existing methods in retrieving relevant frame sequences. Lastly, the proposed method is shown to be capable of processing real-world TFS data with a speed of 2 seconds per second. We define dilation surfaces as a type of surface with a continuous action from the group of scale transformations. A significant portion of this study delves into the dynamics of dilation surfaces that possess horizon saddles. Derivations are also provided in this context for key properties and behaviors associated with transition matrices. It is demonstrated that any surface with an $L^2$ calculation can be characterized as either uniformly hyperbolic or possessing horizon saddles. Consequently, we establish the classification of uniformly hyperbolic dilation surfaces as structures with a $C^0$ structure, based on their transition matrices. Our work includes the development of an algorithm for identifying horizon saddles and calculating scaling rates. This algorithm not only offers a method for verifying smoothing conditions but also facilitates a new approach to detecting hyperbolic properties on a case-by-case basis. Furthermore, we define a new class of surfaces, referred to as weakly Horizontally Uniform, which encompasses previously identified uniformly hyperbolic surfaces. Examples are provided to illustrate the concept of WHU surfaces, as well as cases where the properties of horizon saddles or hyperbolicity are present in non-trivial ways. Finally, through an illustrative example involving a surface derived from a Cantor set, we demonstrate the existence of dilation surfaces possessing both horizon saddles and hyperbolic properties. This example serves as a counterexample to a previously proposed conjecture. Our work also reveals that, in contrast to a different theory, not all surfaces possess a minimal scale factor, with an infinite number of examples that may help shed light on an open problem in this area. Ultimately, the main conclusions of this study hold under the more general assumption that either an infinite number of intersection points or tangent surfaces are present. This condition is, in turn, seen to hold for all known examples in this study. Moreover, we confirm that if a surface possesses a minimal scale factor, then it can be transformed into a C^0 equivalent of a surface with a Horizontally Uniform structure, either through a calculable transition or by removing tangent surfaces. Finally, additional research is proposed which seeks to refine and provide conditions for the occurrence of hyperbolic properties on dilation surfaces without any additional geometric assumptions. Several theories and models, including the generalized Hausdorff dimension and a scaling algorithm for interpolation sets, serve as the foundation for this research. A related but separate area of study, focusing on non-Morse-Smale dynamics of dilation surfaces, is also proposed and explored in a companion paper. A generalized notion of conditioning a Gaussian field on a random index is introduced and explored. The underlying idea is rooted in the standard practice of conditioning a Gaussian field on a $\sigma$-algebra generated by a random variable. However, this approach runs into issues when the field in question is defined on a continuum, as the resulting $\sigma$-algebra proves to be too complex to be well-defined. By instead considering conditioning on a random element of a countable set, these difficulties are mitigated. The existing Replay-Based Methods select experiences randomly, which results in a relatively small influence on the overall training process. In this research, a novel technique called Variance Decrease based Experience Replay, or VDER, is proposed to address this issue. VDER ranks past experiences according to their predicted impact on the current policy, using a minimax strategy to calculate the importance of each experience, which in turn enables more targeted selection of these experiences for Replay. Theoretical justifications for VDER have been established, including proofs related to its optimality and the conditions necessary for its application. The effectiveness of VDER is validated through a range of experiments, including those on discrete and continuous control domains. The outcome of these experiments demonstrates that VDER consistently outperforms existing Replay-Based Methods, resulting in accelerated learning and significantly improved final performance. However, these models have traditionally been based on a basic framework that neglects essential aspects of motion that affect their performance in complex scenarios. In response, we propose a novel method, MoDeRNN, that focuses on capturing the essence of motion and incorporates this information into a recurrent neural network. By including key aspects of motion such as velocity, orientation, and action, MoDeRNN is able to achieve more accurate and realistic predictions on a range of challenging tasks, including multi-target tracking and predicting the paths of self-driving cars. In addition to its practical applications, MoDeRNN also reveals new insights into the characteristics of individual motions and, in a surprising finding, demonstrates that our method is effective even when given incomplete information about the motions, effectively making it a fill-in-the-blinds algorithm. This research focuses on an existing challenge: ensuring data confidentiality when using the JavaScript bridge in.NET to interact with native C++ or native C code. Our solution is to develop a new.NET library named Josephine, which uses JavaScript to manage the lifetime of.NET objects exchanged between the.NET and native worlds. To address the issue of object lifetime management, we combined JavaScript with interop services and created a custom attribute for object wrapping. Our implementation allows us to safely free.NET objects in three scenarios: (i) when a native pointer is no longer accessible in managed code, (ii) when a native pointer is no longer accessible in native code, and (iii) when a wrap is no longer in native code. To demonstrate its performance, we evaluated Josephine on a real-world scenario, showing that it can efficiently manage the lifetime of.NET objects when using the JavaScript bridge without introducing additional overhead. A traditional validation of our earlier findings is presented, revealing connections between quantum calculations and non-commutative Markov processes. The study also yields an interesting application concerning the ranking of projects with uncertain durations and random success rates in the field of finance.

Lastly, a discussion about the potential extension of our findings to the Euclidean duration model is presented, along with the implications for a more intricate theoretical connection between quantum calculations and non-commutative Markov processes in the Euclidean model. 

To facilitate a traditional understanding of our earlier work, an illustration with physical-chemistry project funding is included to demonstrate the applications of quantum calculations based on the linear duration model.

A key component of the framework is the inclusion of a mechanism to explain blockchain transactions, beneficial for assessing the integrity of IoT systems. Additionally, the justification mechanism can be applied across various applications, but its practical development is illustrated through the analysis of a food supply network IoT system. Furthermore, the framework integrates a protocol for managing IoT device lifecycle within the blockchain environment, which is shown to complement the existing framework effectively. Despite the potential benefits, directly applying neural structure learning techniques to shape generation can be challenging due to limited training data and the need for diversity in generated shapes. To address these issues, we propose a novel pipeline for the shape generation of biological cells, leveraging a substantial dataset of electron microscopy images. Our approach involves training a neural network to predict the voxel occupancy values of a 3D grid and then utilizing these voxels to generate diverse cellular shapes through optimization, guided by anatomical constraints. To evaluate our method, we developed and implemented a novel constraint that promotes geometric diversity in generated shapes, based on a metric quantifying cellular topology. Our results demonstrate that the integration of this constraint leads to a substantial increase in generated shape diversity while maintaining top-level quantitative characteristics. Additionally, we compared our method with a variant of latent space modeling approach and found that the generated shapes derived from implicit representations exhibit more accurate quantitative characteristics and higher visual quality. To facilitate research in the field of biological cell generation, we released our source code and the generated cellular shapes dataset, consisting of over 200,000 cellular voxels, which can be accessed at https://sites.google.com/view/cell-shape-generation. Our source code can be found at https://github.com/moebiuswisc/biologic. Our study reveals that implicit models are well-suited for the development of biological cell generation methods due to their ability to naturally accommodate anatomical invariances and generate diverse cellular shapes with accurate quantitative characteristics. To the best of our knowledge, our study represents the first investigation into the application of implicit neural representations for the shape generation of biological cells. Furthermore, our analysis explores the effectiveness of diversity constraints, such as transform consistency, in promoting generated shape diversity. Ultimately, our research aims to make a significant contribution to the advancement of biological cell generation methods, which can lead to the development of more accurate simulation environments for the study of cellular dynamics. While BERT excels at masking language comprehension, its approach can be inefficient
when relying on autoregressive decoding. We present XLNet, a universally consistent
autoregressive pretraining model. In comparison to BERT, our model achieves notable
advances in masking language understanding, as well as significant breakthroughs
in next word prediction and question answering tasks. Notably, in the question
answering domain, our model surpasses the state-of-the-art when evaluated on GLUE
metrics, achieving comparable results to BERT with various pretraining objectives.
Furthermore, our model's performance can be viewed as an improved upper limit
for BERT's masking language understanding ability. Our pretraining strategy is
inspired by the idea of reversing relative sentence directions in the permuted
next sentence prediction task. We also introduce a new version of the true
masked language modeling objective, as well as a pretraining strategy known as
take-one-masking. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhiligeng/XLNet.

The study of exoplanetary atmospheres using transit spectroscopy has significant potential for understanding the composition of these envelopes based on subtle changes in light emitted or absorbed by the planets as they pass in front of their stars. Nonetheless, the characteristic curves resulting from current low-resolution spectroscopy analyses are heavily influenced by the characteristics of the host stars, making it difficult to accurately measure planetary signals. Our study employed synthetic data sets of late-type stars and early-type stars to investigate how stellar traits such as surface temperature, rotation, magnetic field strength, and other factors impact observed spectra. We found that variations in stellar temperature produce the largest differences in planetary signals, with effects typically exceeding those of planetary signals themselves, and resulting in fake curves that deviate from actual signals. We discovered that suppressing stellar characteristics is more effective when using emission spectra as opposed to absorption spectra, with higher-resolution analysis further improving the recovery of planetary signals. Applying high-order Gaussian processes can significantly reduce the impact of stellar features in low-resolution analysis, allowing for more accurate reconstruction of planetary signals, and thereby informing the development of more reliable methods in observational astronomy. Our study utilized synthetic data to evaluate the performance of Gaussian processes under real-world conditions, and demonstrated that this approach is particularly valuable for understanding exoplanetary atmospheres through the analysis of high-resolution emission spectra. Ultimately, our research supports the development of future astronomical missions that prioritize the collection of high-resolution transit spectroscopy, and we propose that demonstrating the applicability of high-order Gaussian processes in actual astronomical data is an essential step toward the successful design and implementation of such missions. Our analysis provides specific guidelines for setting parameters for high-order Gaussian processes in low-resolution spectroscopy, and we anticipate that these findings may additionally find applications in other fields where the technique is employed. Lastly, we propose the establishment of a formalized design and implementation process for future astronomical missions, and proof-of-condea that can alleviate concerns regarding the potential drawbacks, particularly regarding high-resolution requirements. Such concerns include the potential difficulty in achieving high-resolution analysis with existing low-resolution data sets, but our research demonstrates that by focusing on emission spectra, these challenges can be overcome, thereby facilitating the design and implementation of future astronomical missions, and specifically the Plato mission. Our analysis provides specific suggestions for mission designers regarding the optimization of data collection strategies, and we propose the development of more sophisticated models to further inform the design and implementation of future missions, and particularly Plato, which has already undergone this process in accordance with our recommendations. Ultimately, these suggestions may serve as a starting point for future mission design

Our approach also enables the adaptation of stateMENT to various STL robustness definitions, thereby achieving faster computation and higher scalability in practical cyber-physical systems. The efficacy of stateMENT is demonstrated through its application in two significant cyber-physical systems, vehicle platooning and smart traffic management. StateMENT's performance in these examples outshines existing methods, validating its practical application. Furthermore, stateMENT's potential is explored as a differential operator, opening avenues for theoretical cyber-physical system advancements. The presented research and tools enable stateMENT's application across cyber-physical system design, analysis, and development, and its expansion can contribute to new cyber-physical system developments. A general framework for scattering reactions is established, allowing for a relaxed approach to kinematics. We introduce the concept of "laboratory-time", where the trajectory of one particle is mapped against that of its target, regardless of their individual speeds or angles. This "laboratory-time" is plotted against the distance from the axis representing the target's path to create a joint probability distribution for the two particles' paths. We demonstrate the application of this framework to various types of scattering reactions, revealing that the distribution of their trajectories exhibits correlation in the case of elastic scattering, with a phase shift determined by the target's trajectory, as well as an inherent phase shift of π for the case where the particles reverse directions. Furthermore, we show that the distribution of trajectories is distinguishable from that of the target's path alone, with specific conditions allowing for a return to the target's path, known as "target-time", as well as conditions that allow for a complete reversal of the particle's path, leading us to propose the concept of a "topological time" that is invariant across all possible scattering reactions. We also analyze a model of scattering reactions, studying its effects on the distribution of trajectories, as well as the distance between the two paths in the laboratory-time scale, with a re-entrant region, where the distance between the two paths diminishes, emerging from the phase shift analysis. Finally, we explore the potential for this scattering phenomenon to arise from a quantum field theory, with varying degrees of anisotropy in the lattice models as a potential source of this phenomenon. Our findings indicate that the distribution of trajectories is only identical to that of a free particle when there is no anisotropy in the lattice models, with increasing anisotropy leading to a range of possible phase shifts, as determined by the distribution of trajectories itself. We also identify a range of possible distances between the two paths in the laboratory-time scale, with the distance diminishing to zero for certain values of the anisotropy parameter. Our work lays out a general framework for understanding scattering reactions, with a particular emphasis on their trajectories, as well as their potential connections to existing concepts in physics, including "target-time" and "topological time", with further research as an invitation to develop additional insights. By incorporating this contribution, we calculate a modified pressure that arises from blackhole radiation when heated by charged particles and electrons, considering the interactions between these particles in the context of the Casimir effect. Additionally, we explore the electromagnetic radiation in blackbody thermodynamics. Notably, the modified pressure's negative value at negative pressure states signals a phase transition, and further analysis of thermodynamic properties indicates convergence in the presence of Casimir's effect. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the presence of Casimir's effect alters the distinction between high-temperature and low-temperature limits in calculations of entropy, enthalpy, and Gibbs free energy. Visual relocalization is a critical capability for autonomous systems to accurately navigate spaces where GPS signals are weak or unreliable. While 3D geometric information from surfel maps offers a rich framework for navigation, processing huge amounts of geometric data computationally demands significant resources. Consequently, surfel maps often require compression, which may result in subtle inaccuracies that impede visual relocalization techniques. To address this limitation, we introduce a unified framework that integrates a level-set representation and a deep-learned feature descriptor to efficiently tackle compressed 3D surfel maps. By leveraging feature descriptors that minimize pre-training hurdles, our approach facilitates real-time localization on embedded devices. Furthermore, we have developed a global localization module that utilizes a geometric matching pipeline to achieve accurate results, even under challenging conditions. By integrating a geometric module with a descriptor-based feature, our approach significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art visual relocalization techniques. Moreover, our approach's ability to scale has been validated through two different applications: one using synthetic data from a robotic simulation and another using real-world data from a head-mounted display application. To facilitate replication of our results, code and data resources have been made publicly available. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our approach efficiently processes compressed 3D surfel maps with a low feature dimensionality of 64, achieving an average repeat rate of 90%, a repeat 25m away within 1s, and a NEES score of 0.8m. Furthermore, our approach's accuracy using real-world data reaches 99.8% with a median localization delay of 42ms. We believe our approach's capability to navigate spaces with low-precision 3D geometric information will have far-reaching applications in autonomous systems. We plan to explore additional applications, such as SLAM, local feature detection, and tracking, and also expect our work to open up new research avenues in surfel map-assisted navigation. We anticipate that our approach may be extended to support diverse 3D geometric representations and enable real-time visual relocalization in a range of scenarios including self-driving cars, drones, and robotic systems. To date, no such approach has been successfully demonstrated online, and we look forward to implementing and evaluating our approach in real-time online environments in the future. We also intend to adapt our approach to accommodate geometric representations with more structured hierarchies that could potentially yield more accurate results, and also investigate applications in virtual environments where visual consistency could aid geometric reconstruction. Our model incorporates price dependence, limited information, and strategic behavior. We focus on the set of equilibrium outcomes into which prices converge as the number of bidders increases. Key characteristics of this convergence outcome field include: (1) the presence of a special subfield consisting of equilibrium paths derived from the Walrasian auction model; (2) the inclusion of the Walrasian subfield in a broader subfield denoted by $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{Q}}$, consisting of equilibrium paths resulting from the application of the Q procedure; (3) the existence of a unique price function within $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{Q}}$ that serves as a natural limit for the prices achieved as the number of bidders grows; and (4) a special property related to the rates at which prices converge. We identify additional features of this special price function: (5) its equivalence to the equilibrium prices resulting from the Walrasian auction model; (6) its consistency across multiple realization processes; and (7) its potential attainment through the application of a novel auction mechanism. A specific Vassiliev characteristic, known as $q_3$, in the realm of finite type invariants for oriented links has been studied. It can be broken down into two distinct components, which involve a computation based on an integral fox-hatcher loop and a previously computed characteristic, denoted $z_3$. This characteristic, $q_3$, plays a significant role in further developing the structure of the graded vector space that governs the coefficients of the colored Alexander polynomial. This polynomial is derived from a combination of $q_3$ and the double braiding characteristic. Moreover, $q_3$ serves as a key component in establishing that the generating capacity of the vector space, which is used to describe the coefficients of the colored Alexander polynomial, corresponds directly to the volume conjecture of the double branchings invariant as both Vassiliev invariants reach infinite order. Additionally, a specific relationship between $q_3$ and invariants at higher orders can be demonstrated through a computational example in the context of a torus link. Finally, $q_3$ serves as a key component in establishing a formal relationship between the Alexander polynomial and Vassiliev invariants via a formal expansion approach. This relationship is used to derive Colbourn's formula in an analytically simplified context, which relates to a one-form invariant description. In federated learning for classification tasks, several users contribute to the training of a global model by sharing local data and model updates with a central server. This framework is suitable for distributed machine learning scenarios, including smart mobile learning and collaborative educational settings. Current privacy protection methods in federated learning aim to prevent a central server or fellow participants from learning sensitive user information. However, a new form of attack known as pragmatic privacy assault (PPA) has been developed which compromises security even when the first line of defense is activated. PPA differs from conventional machine learning attacks as it utilizes nuanced model behavior data acquired through participation in the federated learning process, specifically aimed at inferring sensitive user information from this participation. Distinguishing it from traditional privacy assaults, PPA does not rely on stolen data but rather analyzes model updates in terms of sensitivity and difficulty to participate in the attack. PPA also exhibits improvements on real-world datasets which surpass state-of-the-art attacks within machine learning and federated learning frameworks. An original attack algorithm has also been introduced which successfully infers sensitive user information from model updates even when the first line of defense is activated. The research further reveals that the first line of defense does not completely safeguard sensitive user information and therefore additional security methods are required. A series of experimental outcomes have also been provided which demonstrate the effectiveness of the PP A attack, specifically showing that the first line of defense does not completely protect sensitive information and therefore PP A remains a threat even with the first line of defense activated. This has significant implications for federated learning frameworks and therefore understanding and preventing PP A attacks is of the utmost importance. Suggestions for mitigating PP A attacks have also been proposed. 

Our work is the first to explore PP A attacks in a formalized context and we have proven that the first line of defense does not completely protect sensitive information from PP A attacks. PP A attacks represent a major challenge to federated learning frameworks and therefore understanding and preventing these attacks is essential to maintaining the security and privacy of sensitive information in such frameworks.

However, this amplifies urban vulnerabilities to cyber threats, necessitating a novel city management approach that leverages cutting-edge urban planning, distributed AI systems, and advanced infrastructure operations, ultimately requiring the strategic deployment of defensive resources during assault scenarios. In this context, our research introduces the Intelligent Urban Defense Game (IUDG), a stylized model for managing defensive strategies against high-stakes, dynamic assaults by sophisticated adversaries. Unlike traditional games, IUDG focuses on adaptive defense planning for urban areas, incorporating uncertain adversary behavior, variable defensive resources, and varying city vulnerability levels. In response, we develop an algorithmic solution, the Incremental Cost Optimizer (ICO), designed to efficiently explore the vast IUDG solution space, consisting of exponential state and action sets, through the principled use of incremental cost functions. Numerical studies on real-world cities, including New York and San Francisco, showcase ICO's effectiveness in finding near-optimal solutions in a timely manner. Through our approach, urban defense planning can be transformed into a tractable problem, paving the way for the creation of intelligent and adaptive urban defense systems, ultimately facilitating effective defensive strategy development and cooperation between adversaries and defenders in an adaptive and protective environment. A software implementation of the IUDG model and associated optimizers is also presented. Our contribution has far-reaching implications, bridging the gaps in urban defense and multi-agent cooperation research fields, offering promising avenues for further investigation. In dynamic environments, an autonomous, wheel-based robot moves along a straight track that periodically changes length in an unpredictable manner. We're investigating how the sudden and unexpected changes in the track's length affect the robot's motion. Although the changes are random, the robot's velocity remains within a certain range, ultimately leading to a uniform distribution of travel times. It's found that the robot consistently moves towards a specific point along the track, known as the "meeting point," and the time it takes to reach this point increases in a predictable manner with distance. By considering the meeting point as an attractive fixed point, we analyze its stability using a mathematical model that describes the robot's motion as a nonlinear transformation. Depending on the frequency of the track's changes and the robot's velocity, two distinct scenarios arise. If the frequency is high enough, the meeting point is an unstable fixed point, causing the robot's distribution of travel times to become bimodal. However, for a lower frequency, the meeting point becomes a locally stable fixed point, and the long-term distribution of the robot's position converges to a symmetric probability distribution, located at a certain distance from the meeting point. By computationally demonstrating this convergence, we're able to mathematically describe the shape of this distribution, known as an "Cauchy distribution." Ultimately, our findings expand the scope of the existing "barrier strategy," allowing its effective use in environments where the track's changes are not limited to a specific range of periods and amplitudes. It's known that a random, low-frequency change can lead to a nearly uniform distribution of travel times, but the current study shows that a higher frequency change can result in a more realistic model of the robot's motion. By incorporating the findings into a representation theory, we're also able to develop a broader "unpredictable shift" strategy, which can be applied in various contexts within the theory. In particular, our approach can be used to create custom distributions of the robot's velocity, a feature not previously considered in the existing research. By incorporating a specific type of force, known as a "white noise drive," into the mathematical model of the robot's motion, we're also able to create a new class of random, periodic solutions that can be applied in a wide range of scenarios within the representation theory. This paper introduces a novel method utilizing natural cubic splines to analyze clinical data from Alzheimer's disease treatment trials. Algebraic representations of linear mixed effects models and repeated measures models provide a basis for this approach. Our approach addresses issues with continuous treatment distribution and provides statistical inferences with appropriate assumptions. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through the comparison of two analyses in a real-world context, one using repeated measures and the other employing mixed effects models. Our results indicate that this method produces reliable point estimates and p-values under various scenarios, including the linear model. Notably, when effect sizes are moderate to strong, the method's output aligns with the repeated measures analysis. In cases of moderate or weak effect sizes, however, the method produces p-values that are overly conservative compared to the repeated measures analysis. The method's implementation is available through the R package AlSpl and demonstrated using Pfizer's phase IIb trial data. Our results show that this trial has a marginally statistically significant effect at 12 weeks, as well as numerically significant results at 6 and 24 weeks. The method's implementation is available through the AlSpl R package, which is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/Pecosblanco/AlSpl. This study is the first to explore the CTSM task, and we create a dataset and conduct thorough evaluations to aid in advancing research in this area. Combinatorial approximations of map ensembles, such as the thermodynamic framework and the TAP framework in statistical mechanics, offer insight into the global behavior of these ensembles. Maps with the same input and output dimensions as the original system are referred to as universal entry frameworks. We explore the possibility of creating simple, polynomial-based universal entry frameworks. In the case of systems with equal input and output dimensions (square systems) and those with an unequal input or output dimension (non-square systems), we identify both existence and non-existence proofs for such frameworks, while considering various parameters and limitations. Our study focuses on enrollments, partial enrollments, biproducts, sub-programs, and limitations, all of which play crucial roles in determining whether a universal entry framework can be constructed. In particular, we show that square systems with specific properties have simple, polynomial-based universal entry frameworks, while non-square systems often lack such frameworks, especially those with certain limitations in biproducts and sub-programs. These findings reveal the intricate characteristics of universal entry frameworks, highlighting their relevance to enrolled ensembles and their potential use in developing and analyzing various physical, chemical, and statistical mechanics models. We also discuss the potential applications of our results to the TAP framework and related issues. Lastly, we provide a summary of open problems and demonstrate how this topic can connect to a broader context. Transformer-based models have achieved remarkable success in various NLP tasks, and several pre-trained models are now publicly available. However, the main issue with these models lies in their inability to leverage the knowledge and structure of downstream tasks, which is crucial for their improved performance. Numerous studies try to unlock the potential of these models by developing innovative methods to infuse task-specific information. Nonetheless, little research explores the fundamental potential of these models when no task-specific information is available. In this paper, we aim to bridge this knowledge gap by proposing a basic benchmark, which only utilizes general linguistic characteristics derived from word frequency. The benchmark's results show that even this simple baseline can achieve competitive performance with many state-of-the-art models that utilize pre-trained models, on several standard learning tasks. Furthermore, our research highlights the significance of understanding the fundamental capabilities of pre-trained models in order to develop more effective methods of utilizing task-specific information. The proposed benchmark is available at https://github.com/fanlanlan/Benchmark-for-Pre-Trained-Models. The experiment results are available at https://l.ningpeng.space/post/sotabench-interpretation/. Our analysis suggests that further investigation into identifying these fundamental capabilities is necessary to unlock the full potential of pre-trained models and ensure their more effective use of task-specific information. The outcome of our research may facilitate the development of more robust and efficient methods of pretraining and downstream model development. Recent advances in automated program patching have shown promising results, but the field is still limited by several challenges. Notably, the space of possible patches is exponentially vast, making space exploration time-consuming and prone to getting stuck in local optimality issues. Moreover, the absence of strong background knowledge in this domain causes transfer learning strategies to struggle. To address these challenges, we propose Antagonistic Patch Learning (APL), an end-to-end trainable repair model that generates two types of patches: a primary patch promoting program execution and an opposing patch preventing it. By leveraging an adversarial training approach, APL learns to recognize the intersection of patches under the guidance of a discriminator that assigns high probabilities to valid programs only. Experimental evaluations on OpenSource and Frep systems demonstrate that APL outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, including a significant improvement in generating fixes for existing programming bugs. Additionally, APL achieves superior results on domain-independent problem solving despite the lack of transfer learning. Notably, APL enhances the understanding of programming skills by learning diverse program representations through encoding various relational aspects at different levels of abstraction. Lastly, APL's constraints on the generation process mirror real-world programming practices found in actual code, making the generated patches applicable to developers in the wild. Key outcomes of our research are three datasets: the Deliberate Programming Dataset, the Fix Prediction Dataset, and the Representational Diversity Dataset, each comprising an extensive collection (100k+ examples) offering valuable resources for programming research in the future. These datasets, along with the code and the Deliberate Programming Challenge, are publicly available at https://apls.ai/experiments.html. An associated video outlining our findings can be accessed at https://youtu.be/8O0YH2r4gKc. Additionally, a companion paper describing APL in detail has been published at IJCAI 2021. Both our work and datasets have received recognition through winning the 2022 AAAI Institutional Data Challenge on Deliberate Programming and the 2021 Dataset of the Year Award at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP). Furthermore, our Deliberate Programming Challenge has ranked 2nd at the 2022 Conference of the Advancement of Scientific Knowledge and 1st at the 2021 Challenge of the Future, both hosted by the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence. Approaching the point of equilibrium in density, atomic nuclei start to exhibit characteristics of a fluid confined within a potential well. Upon increasing the energy density, this fluid undergoes a series of complex changes, beginning with a disordering of its collective movement, followed by the loss of its local stability before eventually flowing freely without constraints. However, the flow's nature remains largely unknown despite its significant influence on the nucleus' state - whether it's a liquid with coordinated movements or chaotic without them. To resolve this ambiguity, researchers rely on examining differential flow quantities, especially vector flow, which provides clarity on the collision structure of the flowing nucleus. The examination also helps in understanding how the flow behaves after the nucleus collides and identifies the non-equilibrium character of the process, as well as its connection to the time-of-flight and impact angle of the target and projectile. The method, heavily rooted in hydrodynamics, is particularly useful in detecting mini-fluid states within low-energy collisions and for analyzing the time-distribution of flow within high-energy impacts. The recent application of this technique to the $\textbf{^{24m5Mg} +^{24m5Mg}}$ system at SU-BRIC has delivered valuable insights - a fragmented final state with non-equilibrium characteristics at an energy density of 0.04 MeV/fm$^3$, where flow is clearly not solely responsible for explaining nuclear radius. The resulting data shows a discrete transition from local equilibrium to non-equilibrium at an energy density of roughly 0.1 keV/fm$^3$. The method also helps in understanding the collision structure of the flowing nucleus at varying energy densities, starting from the isotopic mass of 20 at low energies to a mass of 100 at high energies. The density at which coherent movement ceases to exist is found to be approximately 0.8 times the saturation density at low energies, increasing to 2/3 at intermediate energies and 1/2 at the highest energies. The observation that coherent movement persists even at the most energetic conditions is at odds with the hypothesis of a critical density, while the occurrence of local equilibrium at low energies and non-equilibrium at high energies has a theoretical basis rooted in the hydrodynamic model. The resulting data can be used to identify various states within low-energy collisions - a liquid characterized by out-of-phase radial and tangential movements, another with strong nuclear forces as seen in neutron-star collisions and finally, a case with weak nuclear forces as observed in quark-gluon plasma. The widespread effects of the COVID-19 pandemic highlight the significance of precise epidemiological modeling to guide public health interventions and policy-making. Accurate modeling relies on timely and sensitive repository data, yet advances in machine learning have revealed the peril of data over-exposure, endangering researchers and the community. To address this, a novel approach is presented that utilizes an adversarial network to train a COVID-19 predictor from a German dataset, ensuring model development occurs remotely and is subsequently released along with code for open-source evaluation. Through the integration of an adversarial network, this method surpasses existing baselines in detection accuracy while minimizing data exposure. Moreover, a statistical analysis confirms the model's efficacy in identifying early-stage COVID-19 symptoms. Our results indicate that an accurately trained machine learning model, despite some data loss through label noise, can effectively identify COVID-19 two days sooner than traditional methods, with corresponding statistics available. This research showcases a best practices example for responsible machine learning, particularly in contexts where data-related risks are severe. In recent years, the need for effective spectrum utilization has become increasingly crucial due to the rising demand for wireless services. Spectrally convergent networks are being proposed as a solution, using spectrum-to-application mapping to optimize spectrum utilization, potentially leading to significant performance gains. However, applying this concept to real-world wireless systems is complicated by the high dimensionality and dynamic nature of wireless channel states, making traditional spectrum mapping difficult. To address this challenge, a novel approach is presented, utilizing generalized graph representations and integer reinforcement learning, coupled with a graph neural network decoder to facilitate effective spectrum mapping and optimization. A decentralized reasoning model is also introduced, enabling individual devices to make informed decisions based on collective environmental data. Experimental results demonstrate that this method yields improved spectral efficiency, significantly outperforming existing multiplexing and equal power scheduling techniques. Furthermore, the scalability of this model allows it to effectively tackle the complexities of high-dimensional channel states in large-scale wireless systems. Nonetheless, additional research is required to address potential interoperability concerns in such systems. The proposed approach holds promise for applying spectral convergence theory to real-world wireless systems, paving the way for further research in this direction. Simulation outcomes reveal that in a 10-node network, equal power scheduling falls short of achieving spectral convergence, while the proposed policy achieves a 35.2 dB higher sum rate than equal power scheduling in a 20-node test case. The theoretical spectral convergence rate in a 10-node test case is 0.18, whereas the proposed approach achieves a convergence rate of 0.52. However, in a 100-node test case, equal power scheduling is observed to converge at a rate of 2.0, whereas the proposed approach achieves a convergence rate of 10.0. The proposed model's performance in these test cases surpasses that of various benchmark techniques, including equal power scheduling and theoretical spectral convergence rates.
