Finite element models for analyzing offshore wind turbines' structural behavior are computationally expensive, requiring hours to simulate a single scenario, which limits their use in optimization processes involving multiple scenarios. To address this issue, a probabilistic model was developed that links Gaussian processes to leverage existing models and their associated costs more efficiently. The model was demonstrated by applying it to a previously established model for assessing the impact of wind and waves on an offshore wind turbine's blades, which confirmed its accuracy in matching a finite element model's outcomes with a low margin of error. The model was found to be at least four times faster than the finite element model while preserving a high degree of accuracy, which makes it a viable option for probabilistic optimization processes involving offshore wind turbines. The model was further utilized in a simulation study to investigate its potential in promoting the deployment of wind turbines through the assessment of their stability under various operating conditions. The model was found to be capable of reducing its installed capacity by stopping the turbines from rotating when operating in extreme weather conditions that may lead the turbines to collapse, which could result in significant energy losses and economic losses for the turbines. The model was found to be capable of mitigating these losses by allowing the turbines to continue operating when the weather improves, which could result in considerable gains in terms of capacity factor, which confirms its potential in informing optimization processes involving offshore wind farms. The model was developed within the Python framework, which offers a high level of portability and interoperability with other models, which confirms its practicality in terms of implementation. The model was accompanied by code that was made available for public use, which was run through various benchmarks to verify its performance, which revealed some room for further improvement. Social media monitoring after a disaster enables the evaluation of public's reaction more quickly and accurately compared to conventional survey methods. This study presents an examination of Twitter data related to the 30 July 2020 Izmir earthquake (magnitude 7.8) and resulting fires in Turkey. We conducted a real-time analysis using Twitter data with both sentiment and time series analysis. Our results reveal that sentiment scores fluctuated as new information emerged about the crisis. We also observed a surge in activity on Twitter one day after the earthquake, coinciding with the rescue efforts, and observed via time series analysis that users who shared images without mentioning the earthquake were primarily concerned with the aftermath of the disaster. The results of this study highlight the significance of social media analytics in understanding public opinions and provide valuable insights for decision makers, policy creators, and organizations to target communication more effectively and respond efficiently to crisis situations. The data collected during this study can be potentially used for more informed actions, such as donation, relief supply deliveries, aid provision, and other forms of support. Our work also offers a basis for comparing different relief efforts by analyzing donor engagement, and could be extended to other platforms and applications. The presented findings can contribute to the growth of social media analytics in disaster response and recovery processes, and ultimately aid in supporting crisis communications and management. The presented research and analysis can serve as a basis for developing more effective strategies in using social media for emergency response and management, and facilitating public-private collaboration in crisis situations. The study's results verify the relevance of using social media data in understanding public reactions and providing valuable insights for decision makers, and it is hoped that these outcomes can lead to more accurate and timely analysis of social media data in various applications including crisis management. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that social media monitoring can facilitate conjugation, efficient communication, and effective decision making in the face of emergencies. We anticipate that these study's results will contribute to the development of more efficient and effective disaster response and management strategies, and pave the way for the creation of a more informed and impactful public-private collaboration in crisis situations. We plan to expand on these study's results and continue working on social media analytics for emergency response and management in various applications. Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) have garnered significant research interest due to their potential for widespread wireless coverage and personalized service delivery. However, effective RIS function is heavily dependent on precise channel estimation, which becomes particularly challenging in systems using elementary low complexity systems (ELMs) due to their simplified structure. Current ELM-based channel estimation methods face two primary issues: inadequate utilization of data due to insufficient cyclic prefix (CP) in OFDM systems and inaccurate estimates resulting from analog dysfunction. To tackle these problems, this paper introduces an improved ELM approach, which leverages an optimized data selection algorithm and analog-to-digital conversion model to enhance estimation accuracy. Results show that this proposed method significantly improves channel estimation compared to conventional ones. Furthermore, to address the underutilization of data, this paper suggests utilizing additional data for estimation through an optimized data selection algorithm within the RIS, which also yields substantial improvements in channel estimation. Notably, when both proposals are combined, they lead to a considerable reduction in the mean squared error (MSE) estimate, which is not seen when utilizing large amounts of data in conventional methods. Simulation results confirm the effectiveness of these proposed methods in challenging RIS-supported communication systems. Moreover, when testing these proposals in various scenarios, it was discovered that they can operate effectively in systems using up to 90% reduced CP while remaining relatively resilient to analog dysfunction affecting any ratio of input units to total units. Overall, these proposals have the potential to enhance RIS performance in a wide array of real-world communication systems. Finally, when testing these proposals in an environment with multiple RISs, it was discovered that they can be easily generalized for efficient channel estimation in such systems. Hence, these proposals have the potential to greatly contribute to the development of highly efficient RIS-supported communication systems. The uncertainty principle poses a conundrum that raises the question of whether there exist measurement techniques with infinite precision, a topic central to quantum theory. This problem has connections to both quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics, where the precision of measurements affects our understanding of fluctuations in energy, a key concept in both theories. According to the integral fluctuation theorem, a statistical mechanics principle, one can quantify the likelihood of this precision. However, the same holds true for quantum mechanics, where the possibility of non-invasive measurements enables access to system properties without altering their values. This chapter is dedicated to explaining the relationship between measurement techniques and the fluctuation theorem, focusing on individual constituents within a system as potential targets for non-invasive measurement. Our analysis draws from both quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics, generating two distinct applications of the fluctuation theorem. The first involves individual particles, leading to a formulation of the theorem that accounts for the possibility of non-invasive measurements. The second focuses on the thermodynamic levels of matter and explores the relationship between work statistics, the precision of energy measurements, and fluctuations. It does this within closed systems, where the precision of energy measurements influences the possibility of drawing a thermodynamic representation of a single closed system from its microphysical properties. Our analysis offers insights into the statistical mechanics principle of the fluctuation theorem as well as the connection between quantum mechanics, the uncertainty principle, and this principle. Additionally, it generates a number of theoretical predictions and hypotheses, some of which are experimental in nature and others concerning the interpretation of quantum mechanics. The chapter's primary goal is to demonstrate how the uncertainty principle and the principles of individual measurements, as well as fluctuation theorems, are connected. The chapter also concludes with a discussion on the implications of this connection. The global spread of the coronavirus has prompted numerous countries to adopt a data-driven approach to track its progression, with contact tracing becoming a crucial element in combating the pandemic's advancement. Although contact tracing technology has been deployed in several countries as a key tool in managing the outbreak, concerns have been raised about the privacy implications of using these systems, with users' anonymity a critical factor in their utilization. In this context, we propose an anonymous contact tracing technique, Coronav'SUS, which leverages a hybrid encryption method combining the security of the AES and ElGamal algorithms. Furthermore, we investigate advanced attacks on Coronav'SUS, including linkage, de-annotation, tracing, and tracing-with-leakage attacks, and mitigate them with countermeasures to ensure the anonymity of users utilizing the platform. Through simulation, we evaluate the effectiveness of Coronav'SUS under varying attack conditions and assess its performance in ensuring the privacy of its users. Lastly, we consider the limitations of Coronav'SUS, acknowledging that national health authorities must strike a delicate balance between combating the pandemic and protecting citizens' privacy in the deployment of contact tracing technology. The efficacy of Coronav'SUS illustrates that secure contact tracing can be conducted with relative precision, albeit with varying levels of success depending on the specific attack conditions. In general, we observe that Coronav'SUS achieves satisfactory results in withstanding a wide array of sophisticated attacks, ultimately safeguarding users' confidentiality. The findings of this research ultimately inspire reflections on the deployment of contact tracing technology during public health crises. The implementation code for Coronav'SUS is available at https://github.com/pega12/Coronav'SUS. Recent advancements in quantum machine learning backbones, designed for classical datasets, and quantum circuits, handling quantum data directly or embedding inputs in a classical format, have gained significant attention. Despite much being written about applications, the fundamental differences between classical and quantum data remain underexplored. An examination into these discrepancies is crucial to understanding the unique properties of quantum information and its utilities. In this study, we set out to identify the distinctive attributes of quantum data and investigate how these characteristics affect both quantum machine learning backbones and embedded classical networks. Furthermore, we highlight the implications of these findings on quantum data preprocessing techniques. Through our analysis, we aim to lay the groundwork for leveraging quantitative measures of quantum data properties, which may foster novel approaches to quantum machine learning architectures. We also conduct a preliminary evaluation of these effects by testing simplified models, and our results suggest that quantizing the input can greatly boost the performance of some backbones. The benefits and drawbacks of quantum data properties remain an open area of research, and we raise key questions that drive the forward progress of this emerging field. 

Key Words: quantum data, backbones, embedded circuits, classification, loss functions.

This study investigates the nonrelativistic QCD factorization (NRQCD) method for producing $J/\psi$ mesons via the $e^+e^-$ process, focusing on ${J/\psi+\eta_c,\chi_{cJ}}$ production and including a comparison of leading-order (LO) and next-to-leading-order (NLO) results for decay angle distributions. We found that NLO corrections and radiation fields significantly impact angle distributions, especially at $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV, as they yield smaller NLO corrections compared to LO results. Moreover, we found that NLO corrections reduce the lo discrepancy in the $\cos\theta$ distribution for $J/\psi+\chi_{c0}$ and nearly eliminate it. Finally, we found that higher-order NLO corrections for the $\eta_c(1S)$ differential distribution converge at $\mathcal{O}(1\%)$, suggesting that higher-order NLO corrections may be necessary for more precise measurements. These findings support the feasibility of using ${J/\psi+\eta_c,\chi_{cJ}}$ production at $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV to explore the charm-quark mass through the charm-quark system. This research also lays the groundwork for investigating radiation effects at even higher orders. We have further developed and made our computational code available for the $J/\psi$ production process for potential use in theoretical predictions and future experimental studies. The curvature matrix plays a pivotal role in optimization and variational inference but remains computationally prohibitive due to its high dimensionality. To address this issue, researchers have developed alternative second-order approximations, such as the curvature approximation and Hessian diagonalization. However, these methods lack theoretical guarantees for non-convex problems and do not guarantee approximation of the original curvature matrix. This study establishes theoretical guarantees for a new approximation called ViViT, which can efficiently compute the curvature matrix in various settings. By leveraging the inner-product structure in the gradients, ViViT achieves improved scalability and guarantees for certain types of non-convex problems. Experimental results demonstrate ViViT outperforms existing methods in non-convex settings. Notably, ViViT's theoretical and experimental validation surpasses state-of-the-art methods, such as full Hessian and Gauss-Newton approximation. This research provides a theoretical understanding of the generalized Gauss-Newton's low-dimensional structure and demonstrates that ViViT's dimensionality affects its convergence rate. As a result, this paper sets the foundation for further exploration of the generalized Gauss-Newton's low-dimensional structure. The ViViT method, implemented in Pytorch, is available at https://github.com/huozhi/vi-vit. Furthermore, the findings in this research have been accepted at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2022 under the title "ViViT: Generalized Gauss-Newton's Low-dimensional Structure of Optimization and Variational Inference". A revised version of the paper was published in 2022. The analysis is supported by theoretical proof, experimental results, and graphically illustrated proofs. The main contribution of this research involves demonstrating that ViViT's entry-wise approximation can efficiently compute the curvature matrix, and that the sampling dimension affects the approximation quality. To facilitate understanding, this research provides supplementary analyses, such as proving that the principal sub-matrices remain consistent under noise addition, and that the properties of the inner-product matrix remain preserved even when rows and columns are randomly permuted. In addition, this research investigates an alternative form of approximation, which can efficiently compute the principal sub-matrices, and validates the approximation by proving its accuracy through an analytical comparison. The experimental results presented in this research demonstrate that the approximated principal sub-matrices surpass the existing methods in terms of accuracy. The last contribution of this research lies in validating the theoretical guarantees through experiments, and demonstrating that the theoretical guarantees can be generalized to the case of non-stationary sequences

Many languages differentiate between masculine and feminine forms of nouns, which influences how these nouns are represented. This study is the first to examine how grammatical gender affects word representations in datasets. Analyzing datasets from Spanish, French, and Arabic, we discovered that adding a gender label alongside other features generally doesn't improve predictions, and in some cases, might even make models slightly less accurate. Our findings suggest that embedding gender separately from other features may not always reflect real-world associations between words. This has significant implications for how we design and interpret linguistic representations, particularly in datasets from languages with grammatical gender differentiation. Our code and reports are available for review.

We establish the charmability of finite subgroups of the special linear group and use this property to deduce rigidity. Specifically, it is shown that any deformation of an arithmetic subgroup into a finite subgroup must have constant image. Additionally, this implies that its Lie algebra remains unchanged under any deformation. This result provides implications for the rigidity of actions, including the rigidity of actions on homogeneous spaces. In particular, it is shown that any action on a Euclidean building by a finite subgroup of the general linear group corresponds to a group action. Furthermore, this result yields that some symmetric spaces admit a rigid action, whereas others do not. Notably, this condition holds for G_2-compactifications and certain quotients of SL_2, but not for the 3-sphere or SL_n/J. In a complementary finding, it is demonstrated that torsion-free subgroups of SL_n with small torsion have a non-trivial intersection. These subgroups can potentially form a particular class of solvable groups and their potential charmability is explored. Finally, the non-charmable nature of certain orientable fibrations is established and this property is achieved by constructing a particular cycle that remains invariant under a torus action on a projective space. This result implies that SL_6 does not admit charmability and this property can be generalized to certain virtually abelian groups. However, it is discovered that CL_6 does admit charmability and this property is generalized to certain infinite dihedral groups. Estimating the precise 3D position of objects within images is a crucial element
in numerous applications, including augmented reality, robotics, and human-
machine interaction. Despite advancements in estimating object orientation, the
precise 3D position of objects remains an unsolved problem, particularly when
objects are unidentified or novel categories are introduced. Our study proposes
a novel approach for predicting the 3D position of objects without requiring any
training data on those specific objects. Our approach ensures that the predicted
position is within the boundaries of a virtual 3D model and corresponds to a
valid class-level pose. We evaluate our approach and compare it with existing
methods, and the results can be viewed at https://zshot-pose.github.io. Our
approach also achieves state-of-the-art results on the SCAIL dataset, surpassing
existing methods by a significant margin. Moreover, we introduce a novel
dataset called zePOS, comprising over 13,000 images of 19 categories, each with
multiple objects and objects at various positions. The dataset is available at
https://zenith-pose.github.io. Our approach receives input from a pre-trained
model that identifies objects and predicts their class, allowing us to conduct
zero-shot experiments and assess the generalizability of the results. Our approach
is implemented in the TensorFlow framework and is publicly accessible at
https://github.com/zenith-pose/zshot-pose. Our approach incorporates a unique
regression technique for estimating object position, incorporating constraints
and utilizing Newton's method for convergence. We also introduce a novel cost
function that minimizes the distance between two 3D vectors, yielding results
close to the reference in a collinear manner. Our approach regresses class-level
poses directly without relying on part-level poses, significantly reducing
branching in the predictive model and allowing the application to identify
objects of unseen categories. Our approach expands the scope of existing
models from identified to zero-shot scenarios and is the first to tackle the
zero-shot, object-position estimation problem. Our approach maintains a high
degree of precision in object position estimation and relies on minimal
hyperparameter configuration. Our approach demonstrates successful application
on the zePOS dataset with a low average error of less than 5 cm and an average
orientation error of less than 4.5 degrees at 34 cm distance, surpassing existing
methods by a significant margin. Our approach achieves a 94x reduction in
computational complexity relative to existing methods

Predicting long-term traffic flow is crucial for urban city road networks.
However, existing models face significant challenges due to limited historical
data and the inherent sparsity of traffic flow conditions. Despite these issues,
cities' spatial structure can be leveraged for improving forecasting accuracy.
Therefore, we introduce a novel model called SpaSpa, which utilizes similarity-based
data propagation and an attention-based fusion framework to enhance predicting
future traffic flow. The framework utilizes spatially adjacent regions as references
for data propagation and integrates city's road network features. We evaluate SpaSpa
using real-world data on US road networks and compare its performance to other
state-of-the-art models, showcasing its efficacy in addressing traffic forecasting
sparse data challenges. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of city size and
topology on the performance of SpaSpa, demonstrating its broad applicability. The
source code for SpaSpa is available at https://github.com/fengyunai/SpaSpa. Experimental
results illustrate that SpaSpa surpasses other models in terms of Makovian
predictive accuracy, as well as short-term predictions on traffic flow. An analysis
of the impact of city size and topology on the performance of SpaSpa reveals
variations in model performance, with the model exhibiting a moderate 3.8% loss for
large cities and a notable loss of up to 8% in specific city configurations.
Overall, our research emphasizes the importance of incorporating city's spatial
structure in addressing traffic forecasting's sparse data issue. The SpaSpa model
represent a significant step towards developing city-size agnostic traffic
forecasting models for extensive sparse traffic prediction. Analysis of the model
revels that its performance can be further enhanced through data aggregation from
upper administrative levels of city sizing hierarchies. Such a model would be
beneficial for city urban planners in efficiently utilizing city roads. Ultimately,
our research shows that addressing long-term traffic flow prediction's sparsity
challenge is feasible through leveraging city's spatial structure. SpaSpa presents
a pioneering framework in this direction and has the potential to be extended to
other mobility domains like ride-hailing and bike-sharing. Furthermore, our
analysis highlights that incorporating city's structural features can aid in
addressing the long-term traffic flow prediction's sparsity challenge. Thus, our
research provides a structured approach to developing city-size agnostic traffic

The distribution of fast radio bursts on the European LOFAR network suggests significant FRB populations exist undetected. A scalable capture backend called REALTA was implemented at the Irish LOFAR facility to intercept and digitize radio signals in real-time, allowing for the discovery and analysis of these elusive bursts. Over 45 nights of operation, REALTA recorded 14 distinct FRBs, showcasing its potential for high-sensitivity detections. Notably, three of these FRBs demonstrated significant bandwidth, exhibiting multiple-signal patterns, while the others displayed single-peaked structures. Moreover, REALTA detected a recurring FRB candidate, marking the first instance of repeated observations from the LOFAR network. Our data collection is expected to expand significantly, potentially yielding a comprehensive FRB population over an extensive period. In addition to FRB detection, REALTA's capabilities may also encompass the observation of other transient phenomena, such as GRB early bursts, Giant Pulses, and Pulsar irregularities. A future upgrade could incorporate artificial intelligence-based algorithms to automate the detection process, further enhancing both REALTA's potential and the LOFAR network's. A proposed upgrade to a 8-bit ADC with increased sampling rates to 2.4 ns will significantly expand the detectable pulse arrival time range, while a planned memory expansion will facilitate offline analysis of up to 14 days of continuous data, greatly surpassing its current 45-minute capability. Moreover, a new LOFAR station in N Ireland is under construction which will greatly expand the field of view allowing for the detection of more FRBs and transients. When operational, a ring configuration incorporating all 50 individual antennas from LOFAR stations across 10 countries will significantly amplify a pulsar's signal, enabling detection even when the pulse width becomes as narrow as 30 Hz. Notably, a planned upgrade of the data processing architecture will allow REALTA to detect individual pulses from distant pulsars with the LOFAR network, a task currently beyond its capabilities. A future generation LOFAR-like network called NISP is also under development. NISP will nearly double the number of antennas and expand the frequency range to a neighboring band above 1 GHz, allowing for detection of very short and potentially periodical pulses. A planned LOFAR successor, the Square Kilometre Array, will further expand the scale when it comes online in 2027. A cutting-edge neural network model, known as DNN, plays a vital role in the modern entertainment industry for predicting box office revenue, a phenomenon that has become known as "opening-day/week forecasting." Despite advancements in large datasets and the use of advanced mathematical models, the box office prediction remains a challenging task due to the complex interplay of underlying variables. This study leverages a large, 3056-sample film dataset that includes successful opening weekends and gross incomes from  2018-2020, and utilizes an extensive collection of character, tone, and action features extracted before analyzing the data. By comparing models with and without pre-released features, we highlight their respective advantages and explore their impact on forecast accuracy. Our results reveal that incorporating pre-released features enables significant improvement in prediction outcomes, and that integrating these features into existing models can broaden their applicability and result in more accurate box office revenue predictions. Additionally, our investigation into the pre-released features themselves allows us to draw a comparative analysis of the opening weekends and financial successes of highly successful films like "Avengers: Endgame" and "Breakfast at Sweethill." Ultimately, our study confirms the value of utilizing large datasets and pre-released features in box office prediction. Both the complete film dataset and pre-released features used in this study are available for download on the GitHub platform.

We propose a novel approach to quantum betting based on Kelly wagering, allowing us to determine the optimal stake amount in terms of qubits for a given outcome probability, which can be scaled up for multiple-round wagers. This formula serves as a fundamental principle in information theory, optimizing long-term growth in wealth through consistent betting strategies. We also outline the framework for implementing this concept in experiments, utilizing continuous-variable methods, and provide a preliminary analysis of a protocol based on linear-amplitude optical quantum computing. Furthermore, we examine an extension of this principle in contexts where the betting outcome is dependent on private information (known as betting with an edge), revealing a simplified means of achieving long-term wealth maximization within this framework. However, in certain scenarios where the information gap increases at a decreasing rate (convergent 'edge'), the traditional Kelly betting formula falls short, failing to adequately compute the optimal stake amount. We verify this through both analytical calculations and numerical simulations. To address this limitation, we present an adapted betting formula tailored to scenarios with a convergent 'edge' and demonstrate its greater accuracy in such instances. Ultimately, we analyze scenarios in which either the 'edge' or winning probability is fixed. In the first, we provide a comprehensive analysis, while in the latter, we offer a preliminary investigation accompanied by numerical results. Our work equips individuals working within linear-amplitude optical quantum computing with the necessary tools to execute betting experiments that have proven effective in simulations. This research may also be applied to other fields where the Kelly wagering principle applies. We conclude by exploring potential avenues for experimentation in thermal storage and conversion, as well as thermophotonic betting. Lastly, we provide a note on the potential for a real-world application of quantum betting by replicating a protocol in line with the principles of notational PAQ* and NISQ. The remarkable success of large-scale image classification models has made them an essential component in our daily lives. Notably, computer vision has been pivotal in shaping our understanding of people's appearance, particularly in the legal system. Nevertheless, there is still a significant divide between the quality of pre-trained models for individuals from diverse backgrounds and those with larger, more representative datasets. Notably, face recognition technology has been applied in justice systems across the world, despite potential biases, to identify suspects based on security camera images. The European Court of Human Rights has raised concerns about the risk of errors in face recognition-based identifications, and a leading research institution has proposed training models specifically for specific courts to mitigate bias, an approach dubbed "justice-aware" modeling. Similar to other context-specific models, this approach requires adapting federated learning, a technique allowing the simultaneous training of models by multiple entities using only local data, to be feasible. Notably, when applied to face identification, this technique compromises the confidentiality of images, which may lead to severe consequences. To address this challenge, we have developed an innovative method for training models in the face recognition domain that incorporates two key principles: utilizing complex network architecture designs to reduce the diffusion of sensitive information and applying differential privacy to ensure that the resulting models do not expose the contents of the training images. Notably, the resulting approach leads to a notable drop in accuracy when tested on identification benchmarks, an average loss of 8.2% for various justice-specific and general identification benchmarks, along with an average increase in privacy loss of 71.6% as measured by the risk metric. Moreover, the approach leads to a notable decrease in the effect of biases in the training data on the model's performance, as evidenced by models with a 6.2% reduced bias on the Columbia GAN dataset. We believe that the innovation lies in the technical design, specifically in the innovation of the approach itself, which abstracts away from specific justice-specific models and is thus applicable to any other context. In recent years, intelligent reflecting surfaces have been proposed as a promising technology to manage wireless communication networks and reconfigure the properties of radio waves. Due to its numerous benefits, IRS has gained significant interest in the research community. An IRS-assisted system that combines energy harvesting and disruption in a two-node communication system is investigated in this study. The system works by having a transmitter continuously send out messages, with a receiver that can harness energy from the incoming signals if needed, though the receiver prioritizes using the strongest signal. Meanwhile, the sender may also receive energy from time to time. The aim is to maximize the total system throughput by adjusting IRS elements, except for a fixed number which remain set to a predefined value. A sophisticated, low-resource-trained function is employed to forecast the optimal values of various IRS elements, such as amplification factors, phase shifts, and time of activation, per unit time, for maximum throughput. The performance of this technique is compared with other machine learning-based methods, including two variants that only predict either amplification factors or a combination of both, in addition to a benchmark approach that uses detailed system models to make predictions. The numerical results demonstrate that our proposed solution boasts superior performance in terms of achieved throughput across different scenarios, while also showing great accuracy by comparing predicted and actual values. Additionally, our method requires significantly fewer training data samples than comparable machine learning-based methods, leading to a substantial decrease in computation time, thus showcasing its impressive capabilities. The computational complexity of this method has also been calculated and analyzed. The findings suggest that our method performs well under different situations and outperforms other tested approaches which only use partial information. Moreover, our method performs well which uses detailed models to make predictions. The proposed solution can successfully assist in optimizing the performance of IRS-assisted systems, even in cases where only a small number of parameters are known in advance. Our study also highlights several areas where further research is needed to fine-tune the performance of IRS-assisted systems, thus showcasing its practical applications in real-world scenarios. Our investigation reveals that the employment of an incremental and shared technique for generating architectures within the NAS method leads to a significant reduction in interruption and subsequently allows for a more in-depth analysis. Furthermore, we analyze the correlation between an architecture's performance and expenses, and we propose an approach for estimating performance expenses of architectures, which can function independently and concurrently with a search method that is cost effective. Ultimately, we conduct an in-depth analysis of our approach on the ImageNet dataset and achieve a level of performance comparable to DARTS, despite occupying only approximately 5% to 9% of its parameter budget. Our source code is accessible via github.com/auditor-at/nas-cost. Our method has demonstrated superiority over other approaches in terms of its expense standards, and we believe that an in-depth examination of its interruption characteristics yields an insightful understanding, which can lead to a more effective approach for reducing interruption in the future. Time series analysis is a vital aspect of modern science, featuring a broad range of applications from weather forecasting to pandemic surveillance. This type of data is typically characterized by temporal dimension, offering valuable insights into underlying systems. Despite their importance, proper analysis requires a range of advanced techniques, including feature extraction and multi-variable comparison, which can be challenging to execute. This challenge stems not only from the inherent properties of time series data but also from the lack of a unified software integration platform that can easily implement time series operations. To address this issue, we have developed a comprehensive R package called theft that provides a cohesive framework for executing a variety of time series tasks. This document showcases the package's functionality for handling attribute-based time series analysis. Additionally, we have created a theft package user guide that covers both attribute-based and abductive time series analysis. Users can access this guide at https://thesmithgroup.github.io/threat/. 

The following time series tasks are demonstrated in this guide and illustrated through example cases:

1.  Multi-variable parallel coordination plots for simultaneous comparison of four variables.
2  Multi-variable comparison using box plots to assess variability among multiple series.
3  Custom time series feature extraction, including mean, standard deviation, and quantiles.
4  Independent component analysis with corresponding plots.
5  One-dimensional time series reduction via singular spectrum analysis.
6  Two-dimensional time series reduction with PCA or FA.
7  Three-dimensional time series reduction with PCA or FA.
8  Five-dimensional time series reduction with PCA or FA.

All examples are showcased using data from the COVID-19 pandemic. 

It's worth to note that the package is not only applicable for attribute-based time series analysis but also for a broad range of general time series tasks with following features:

*  Multivariate data support
*  Independent component analysis
*  Singular spectrum analysis
*  Feature extraction with several built-in time series statistics
*  1D, 2D, 3D time series reduction with PCA, FA methods

This paper introduces an approach that utilizes learning from observations to assess the reliability of translators. It challenges a fundamental assumption in reliability assessment, namely that judgments from expert sources are unbiased. Our approach is grounded in the principle that assessing a system's reliability entails identifying its trustworthy components, but translating such a task proves difficult due to the linguistic barrier, making translation an untrustworthy component in reliability assessment. Furthermore, most conventional methods struggle to account for discrepancies between individual expert judgments and the average, resulting in unreliable estimates. To address these issues, we developed a Bayesian-based evaluation method that distinguishes reliable translators from unreliable ones by learning an ideal translator's profile in an iterative process, incorporating various reliable indicators of translation consistency. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of our method, highlighting its distinction between reliable and unreliable translators. Moreover, we discovered that utilising expert judges' opinions, like other traditional metrics, often results in unreliable estimates due to significant discrepancies between individuals, while utilising consensus-based evaluation can provide more reliable results. Our method's reliability is highlighted through a comparative study with a conventional metric, showing its significantly lower variation among consensus translators. Finally, through a case study of NLPN's translation, our method revealed that some translators are unreliable, providing valuable feedback for users and suggesting the deployment of our method as an essential dependability evaluation tool. Recent discoveries about the inherent properties of wave systems have included Mie scattering and novel optical experiments.  Key to these findings were the interference patterns, or eigenchannels, derived from solving unitary problems.  While the principles that govern total absorption and nonlinearity in these systems have been well-researched, less is known about a general principle that connects them in a unitary framework.  Our study provides four novel results which demonstrate the relationship between energy absorption and nonlinearity in scattering problems.  Specifically, we show that (1) the sum of absorption eigenchannels' nonlinearity is equal to the system's overall nonlinearity, (2) this sum is independent of the reference frame, (3) this principle applies to systems where scattering is non-uniform and (4) similar principles can be found in systems where the unitary problem involves rotation.  Our research verifies these findings through numerical simulations and offers insights based on previous studies about the relationship between interference patterns and system properties.  These results have significant implications for the strategies used to design and engineer interference eigenchannels.  Our study also opens the door for the discovery of novel relationships between interference patterns and system properties in diverse contexts. Our research explores the concept of "winning lottery tickets" within neural networks and examines their underlying properties. We utilize the idea that smaller sub-networks within fully connected ones may hold the key to their predictive potential. Through an iterative trimming procedure, we're able to significantly reduce the size of the network while maintaining, and even enhancing, the model's performance. This process identifies crucial elements at each stage and removes non-essential ones, much like sifting through options. Our findings suggest that convolutional networks already possess advantageous characteristics, as trimming them doesn't lead to further improvements, indicating that the remaining parts are essentially "optimal" tickets. However, by employing an unbiased trimming method on a fully connected network with similar architecture, we're able to isolate the most critical components and replace non-essential parts with better performing ones, resulting in a substantial boost to accuracy. These insights expand our understanding of lottery tickets and provide a significant step towards simplifying neural networks, potentially accelerating training times and achieving smoother results. Our unique trimming algorithm allows us to carefully reduce the size of the network, thereby recovering, and even surpassing, the performance of the original fully connected model, using up to 60% less parameters than the original. What's more, we're able to achieve this improvement while retaining the ability to modify the parameters, thereby validating the true potential of the neural network. This research documents an innovative algorithm for uncovering the hidden, optimized sub-networks within larger, unoptimized ones, thereby enabling us to transform our understanding of the commonly held view that larger networks are generally better. Our results demonstrate that the size of the network does not directly determine the performance, thereby shedding new light on this common assumption. Our work also provides a mathematical understanding of the trimming algorithm, as well as a theoretical basis for its success, potentially paving the way for further advancements in the field. Our unique approach also allows us to carefully reduce the size of the network while maintaining, and enhancing, the model's capacity for generalization, thereby accelerating the training process, enhancing effectiveness, and simplifying the development of transfer learning strategies in the long run. Our theoretical findings provide a mathematical explanation for the success of the trimming algorithm, potentially validating its effectiveness not only on other datasets but also for other future algorithms. Our approach has also inspired an abstract perspective on regularisation, suggesting that the size of the network, rather than the amount of parameters, is the key determinant of the regularisation effect. This perspective holds significant potential for simplifying the development of regularisation strategies in the future

t-SNE, a popular dimensionality reduction technique, is widely employed to visualize and analyze data in lower dimensions, but it assumes a Gaussian process. In many cases, data follows a more suitable multivariate von Mises-Fisher (VMF) distribution, particularly for spherical data. However, there aren't any established methods for performing t-SNE on such data. In this research, we derive a precise formula for transforming VMF distributions into Gaussian distributions, which is the foundation of t-SNE. We introduce a novel, efficient method, VMF-SNE, which applies a pseudo-Gaussian t-SNE to VMF data on a sphere. Our experiments show that VMF-SNE outperforms the standard Gaussian t-SNE. Moreover, we integrate VMF-SNE into a deep learning framework, which trains pseudo-Gaussian distributions to map high-dimensional VMF data onto lower dimensional, non-Euclidean sphere-like spaces. Our method, named Deep VMF-SNE, produces more accurate results than its predecessor, Gaussian Embeddings. When applied to 3D deep learning datasets, Deep VMF-SNE improves the classification performance compared to Gaussian Embeddings. Our code for VMF-SNE and Deep VMF-SNE has been made publicly available.  Our research offers novel, accurate techniques for dimensionality reduction and deep learning on VMF datasets in low and high dimensions, respectively. Additionally, we provide a detailed, straightforward introduction to t-SNE for users working with VMF distributions. Our work is the first to explore t-SNE on VMF distributions, resulting in a contribution to the field of dimensionality reduction and visualization. In particular, our methods are applicable to a broad range of datasets, including those with varying degrees of spherical structure. In this study, we examined the feasibility of simulating Fermi systems on a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing platform. To model Fermi systems, we developed an algorithm to create a Fermi-Hubbard Hamiltonian based on a quantum bosonic system. This involved converting fermions into a bosonic model by utilizing two-mode bosonic oscillators and applying a simultaneous canonical transformation. Our results demonstrate that a sufficient bosonic representation of the Fermi-Hubbard model can be achieved with a polynomial increase in the number of bosonic modes, independent of the system size. Additionally, we devised a quantum computing scheme to implement the bosonic representation and assessed its analog quantum computing feasibility. Our findings suggest that simulating Fermi systems on a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing platform is feasible with current technology, given that a relatively small number of additional analog gates and a large coherence time are required. To achieve this, we propose a hybrid approach, integrating both digital and analog quantum gates. We performed a cost analysis and found that the analog quantum gates contribute a manageable portion to the overall error budget, resulting in an acceptable level of imperfection. We concluded that digital-analog simulation of Fermi systems is a viable option, provided that the analog quantum gates can be optimized to be as few in number as possible. Finally, we conducted a model case study to verify that simulating Fermi systems using the proposed approach yields accurate results, matching the outcomes of exact diagonalization calculations. This successful study enhances the potential of digital-analog simulation in tackling complex, interacting many-body Fermi systems. The code for our analysis is openly available on the GitHub repository specified. Moreover, our proposed method could be adapted to simulate other bosonic models, such as the superconducting circuit-based Kitaev chain model, by converting fermions into a system of coupled tunable oscillators. We believe that our research may lead to the development of a stable, integrated digital-analog simulator in the near future. Such a device would allow physicists to study complex many-body Fermi systems, thereby accelerating theoretical developments in condensed matter physics, chemistry, and materials science. Furthermore, our approach could be applied to simulate the dynamics of Fermi systems using variational quantum algorithms, such as VQE, to determine the ground state and perform quantum simulations. A graph polynomial is considered a element of a broader class if its coefficients form an integer sequence that can be represented by a single infinite series of polynomials, over a stable interval that applies to graphs of any given size. In such a scenario, the number of such polynomial series is infinite, but a particular instance can be identified for basic graph invariants, including the characteristic polynomial, the chromatic polynomial, the flow polynomial, and others. These polynomial series play a significant role in summarizing a graph's properties and are used to develop recursive formulas, identify normal forms, and establish relationships with other invariants. The discussion will focus on constructing these polynomial series for the mentioned invariants and exploring their significance in graph theory. The presentation will involve a review of previously known results and an overview of open questions and potential areas for further research. Ultimately, the discussion will lie in the realm of theoretical graph theory. The minimum uncertainty limit is a fundamental concept that minimizes the product of uncertainties in two variables. This minimum uncertainty limit is a broad principle that goes beyond the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. This article explores the generalized uncertainty limit in the context of Galilean and Lorentz transformations. We examine the relationship between position and momentum, as well as the relationship between time and energy, subject to these transformations. In addition, we provide mathematical proofs to confirm that the minimum uncertainty limit does not violate either the Galilean or Lorentz principle. This implies that introducing a minimum uncertainty limit does not provide a fresh insight that contradicts established physical principles. We also discuss the implications of the generalized uncertainty limit on the product of position and momentum, as well as the product of time and energy. Furthermore, we evaluate the minimum uncertainty limit in the context of the Lorentz transformation, focusing on particular cases where a minimum uncertainty limit can be meaningful. This study reveals that, under specific conditions, introducing a minimum uncertainty limit can have meaningful physical consequences, even within the context of the Lorentz transformation. As an example, we consider the case of a particle moving at a speed close to the speed of light within a galaxy that is moving toward a stationary galaxy. We analyze the implications for a particle moving a short distance in the moving galaxy and demonstrate that, in certain scenarios, the product of time and energy may approach specific values related to the speed of light and the galaxy's velocity with respect to the stationary galaxy. Finally, this study concludes that the minimum uncertainty limit is a broad principle that does not provide fresh insights into the established laws of physics, except in specific cases with particular numerical values, which may lack significance. Even for relativistic velocities close to the speed of light, introducing a minimum uncertainty limit does not result in numerical values that differ substantially from one another. As an example, for a particle moving a short distance in the moving galaxy, the product of time and energy may approach specific values related to the speed of light and the galaxy's velocity with respect to the stationary galaxy, which differ from each other by a small ratio. Therefore, this minimum uncertainty limit does not appear to be useful in predicting numerical values that are significantly different from one another, which may be necessary for making precise predictions in various applications. Additionally, we introduce a new theoretical model that enables a realistic simulation of various forms of noise that may affect both input states and measurement outcomes in quantum classifiers. Mobile cellular network radio transmissions can be heavily disrupted by their own infrastructure if proper accounting for their transmission patterns is not made during network planning. In order to prevent this, the primary approach involves using data collected from the network and training it using machine learning. In our research, we leverage advanced deep convolutional neural network architectures to model radio transmissions, specifically when a device is actively sending data, based solely on recorded activity patterns over time. We evaluate two pre-existing models - one Sigmoid and another Softmax - in addition to introducing a Class Convolution and a Sequential Convolution architecture. In our study, we analyze and compare the effectiveness of these models on both urban and rural environments, utilizing recordings from 21 distinct sites. Our findings suggest that the Class Convolution architecture offers the best performance, producing results that are remarkably close to perfect recall, even performing well when given data from only a fraction of devices in the network. Overall, the Class Convolution architecture offers benefits in terms of both simplicity and efficiency, making it an ideal solution for real-world implementation. Furthermore, our study presents an original approach to analyzing and visualizing machine learning performance, leveraging contingency matrix data, precision and recall metrics, and comprehensive numerical analysis. Additionally, we provide a step-by-step guide on seamlessly integrating CNN models into the spatial statistics methodology used for network planning. In our study, we also demonstrate that leveraging data augmentation allows for significant improvement in the models' ability to accurately distinguish between active and inactive devices, particularly when considering a training strategy involving multiple steps. Finally, the sample data and a detailed tutorial on replicating our study are publicly available on our website. Both the tutorial and dataset can serve as valuable resources for researchers and practitioners in the field. The primary tutorial consists of a multi-part guide titled Convolutional Neural Networks for Radio Event Detection. The tutorial is part of a larger project titled Cellular Network Radio Event Detection with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks. Multi-century projections of future energy systems, required for assessing mitigation strategies and evaluating climate policy, rely on intricate models that consider interplay between energy systems and their socio-economic underpinnings. Yet, due to a lack of historical data, these models face significant hurdles in testing. Consequently, the ability to thoroughly validate these long-term models and choose the most accurate ones remains limited. This study addresses this challenge by employing a novel approach that estimates the accuracy of past model predictions, rather than solely evaluating their consistency with historical data. We then utilize this approach for a group of models that forecast future energy systems, revealing important insights into model performance assessment. Notably, our results indicate that current models are susceptible to various socio-economic trends, which complicates their evaluation. Additionally, our analysis confirms that models with opposing energy system growth scenarios cannot be evaluated through simple statistical comparisons with historical data. However, our method does allow for a semi-quantitative assessment of models that provide far-sighted projections of future energy systems, by considering (1) the alignment of their growth patterns with observed trends, and (2) the consistency of their growth patterns over time. We demonstrate that this approach provides meaningful rankings of models yet to be tested, and offers key insights into the characteristics of future energy systems, which can be used to inform climate policy discussions. Although the scope of this study is energy systems, the method can be applied to any situation requiring long-term forecasting. Furthermore, our analysis highlights some inherent limitations in model performance assessment, primarily stemming from the constraints of using the past to predict the future. We argue that future research should target two main goals: first, the development of better near-far-future observations, and second, the design of a more robust model performance assessment method that does not solely rely on the past. By achieving these objectives, we can break free from the limitations of historical data and temporarily divert from the scientific mantra of 'the more data, the better'. Ultimately, this study offers a temporary solution until more comprehensive growth scenarios become available. We estimate that this could happen around the middle of the 22nd century, marking the transition from the past to a truly long-term future - a century indeed far, yet hopeful. We examine well-posedness for Vlasov-type systems combining a Vlasov equation with a Poisson-type autorepulsive force in limited areas of $\mathbb{R}^d$ with bounded walls. Our key assumption is that the boundary interaction has a certain form, leading to a specific singularity in the far field of macroscopic velocities, which enables us to demonstrate strict stability of the stationary solution represented by a uniform gas against small perturbations at the boundary. Furthermore, under these conditions, we prove the worldwide existence of non-negative solutions to the Vlasov-Poisson-RCK system, a model studying the dynamics of quasi-one-dimensional particle systems with repulsive forces. Additionally, we establish an analogue of the classic Hinze variational integrator for weak solutions of the Vlasov-Poisson system in confined domains with a perfect example of a computable repulsive potential that fulfills our conditions. Lastly, we show the long-term strict contraction of a weakly dissipative Vlasov-Poisson system in a space of measured functions towards the uniform gas. These results are seen as a form of worldwide well-posedness for Vlasov-type systems combining a Vlasov equation with a Poisson-type autorepulsive force in limited areas. In various contexts such as both human and machine reading, a stem document (such as a textbook, scientific article) can be defined as an authoritative source of information. Understanding the document's category is crucial for pinpointing relevant documents and synthesizing knowledge. Although categorization has been successful in some cases, the varying vocabulary used by different authors as well as changes in word meanings over time causes challenges in both human and machine learning models. Theories from Cognitive Linguistics, specifically the Conceptual Metaphor Theory and Grounded Cognition, imply that meaning is tied to context rather than rigid categories, potentially resolving the issue of word sense ambiguity. Moreover, mathematical entities such as equations play a pivotal role in understanding STEM concepts, mainly due to their explicit nature. By establishing relationships between explicit mathematical entities and implicit conceptual entities (such as vectors, points) in a stem document, we aim to demonstrate their influence on categorization models. Through the application of a connectionist shift graph approach that captures both explicit and implicit relationships, we can evaluate its potential in documenting the gradual shift in concept categories over time as seen in a stem document. The results show that incorporating structural relationships between STEM concepts from mathematics helps readers and machine readers to infer the category of an unknown document. The method has been successfully tested using a crowd-sourced labeling dataset from edX and MOOC courses, and its practical implications are explored through discussion. Mechanism design research has a long-standing challenge of creating auctions that are resistant to strategic bidders and optimized for high revenue. To address this issue, we focus on the reliable matching problem within this broader context. In a fair and honest online matching market, each seller and buyer submit preferences over potential matches at regular intervals. Our goal is to develop an algorithm that ensures optimal matching while allowing participants to make informed decisions about when to submit preferences. We introduce the concept of reliable matching and establish a criterion for evaluating such algorithms. We also investigate the possibilities of making optimal matches in specific scenarios, even when bidders engage in strategic behavior. Our study features an extensive analysis of how the probability of achieving optimal matches changes in response to varying market conditions. We propose an offer-making algorithm that strikes a balance between submitting preferences and achieving high matching rates, taking into account both the total number of submissions and time intervals. We assess the performance of our algorithm using both synthetic data and a dataset based on ride-sharing services. Our findings suggest that by controlling the number of submissions, rather than time intervals, we can maximize the probability of making optimal matches in markets with multiple sellers and buyers. Furthermore, by leveraging the total number of submissions instead of individual intervals, we can achieve optimal matches in markets with a large number of buyers. Our analysis also reveals that by limiting submissions, we can achieve optimal matches in markets with varying levels of density. We observe similar patterns in the synthetic data, in addition to finding that the optimal time to submit preferences varies based on the specific problem being considered, while the total number of submissions remains relevant across different problem variants. Using the ride-sharing dataset, we confirm that pre-scheduling and avoiding last-minute submissions can enhance the quality of matches within the sharing economy. Our study provides a framework for understanding the trade-offs between submission frequency and matching quality, as well as suggesting that by limiting submissions, individuals can still achieve optimal matches in various online matching scenarios. Our algorithm demonstrates a 77.9% matching rate for sellers and 81.4% rate for buyers on ride-sharing data, compared to an optimal rate of 82.3% for sellers and 82.6% for buyers in the synthetic data, outperforming many other variants of the algorithm we tested. Our analysis highlights that by varying the total number of submissions, we can control the algorithm's matching rate in online matching problems. We also find that by leveraging submission data, even when bidders engage in strategic behavior, we can still achieve optimal revenue within specific revenue-optimal auction designs

To address this limitation, a novel cross encoder model called SummScore was introduced, offering an all-encompassing evaluation method. This approach was trained on diverse datasets such as DeSe, SmartSumm, DeSe+SummFC, and CNN/DailyMail, and outperformed existing metrics in several scenarios. Moreover, SummScore was utilized to evaluate current summarization systems and found them to be suboptimal when compared to the performance of the proposed metric. To facilitate its adoption, the SummScore model, training data, and related tools have been made publicly available for researchers and developers. Furthermore, based on the effectiveness of SummScore, we suggest integrating it into Google's autoevaluator, as well as developing tools for assessing multilingual summarization and detecting generated text. Lastly, we provide a thorough analysis of the potential drawbacks of the proposed metric, accompanied by a plan for the incorporation of additional qualities that enhance summarization performance, such as coherence, following a structure inspired by the NEOAFL* checklist for NLP system development and evaluation. This research aims to establish a higher standard for NLP innovation assessment. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive evaluation of an NLP system development and evaluation metric. To facilitate its use, we also provide a set of frequently asked questions and demonstrate its functionality through a corresponding Jupyter notebook. Investigations into nonlinear fluid dynamics, covered by the broad term "fluid dynamics," encompass a wide scope of complex interactions between fluids and light, as well as fluid-borne solitons and their interactions with the surrounding fluid and ambient light. This broad term can be broken down into two subcategories: the examination of how fluids move and the examination of how light behaves within fluids. Researchers now have the capability to directly observe and study the behavior of nonlinear processes in fluids through the utilization of advanced experimental techniques. However, the behavior of light within fluids is influenced by an intricate interplay of thermally-induced scatterance and absorption. In turn, this leads to the appearance of various and often unexpected phenomena in liquids, such as laser-generated autoregression, absorption, emission, and nonlinear diffraction patterns that are challenging to forecast. In specific circumstances, when the intensity of the light surpasses a particular threshold, the liquid may absorb sufficient energy to its interior, resulting in the generation of thermal gradients that can impart a time-dependent variation in thermally-induced scatterance. In such cases, observers may observe time-dependent variations in the diffraction patterns, confusingly suggesting a connection to autoregression, when in fact they are a result of a fundamental discrepancy between the timing of the variations in thermally-induced scatterance and the variations in the observed diffraction patterns. In order to distinguish between these processes, researchers must be aware of the role of thermally-induced scatterance and utilize numerical methods capable of simulating both absorption and thermally-induced scatterance. This work involves a detailed numerical description of the thermal profiles within liquids under specific ambient conditions, when subjected to the stress of a tightly focused laser beam, leading to the observation of intricate nonlinear diffraction patterns that are a result of a combination of both absorption and thermally-induced scatterance. During the requirements gathering stage, developers aim to grasp users' actual needs by engaging in "design conversations". To assist in this process, our system employs natural language and domain knowledge to generate possible design options in the form of user stories. Utilizing a constructed corpus of 617 user stories from 14 software projects, our system aims to provide developers with additional perspective to enhance their design considerations. To evaluate conversation quality, particularly conclusions, our model was applied to 120 user stories without prior training. Results indicate that conclusions lacking are quite common, while when present, they demonstrate notable conclusions stability. Moreover, manually examining the transcripts of a discussion with users, our system can automatically produce conclusions consistent with user intentions. Overall, our system demonstrates conclusions stability as a valuable resource for designers to consider during conversations. To promote further advancements in this area, we suggest considering low-resource sequence-to-sequence systems as an alternative to fine-tuning models like T5, and investigating how to facilitate user intentions transparency in system conclusions. The introduction of a new framework, H-STREAM, aims to integrate established stream processing operators to develop scalable and efficient analytical pipelines for real-time and online decision-making processes. Built on a hierarchical data model, H-STREAM allows for the representation of complex time-series data formats such as time-stamped semi-structured data and time-stamped pseudo-records. The framework provides comprehensive data management and querying capabilities, supporting both aggregate-based and event-based query processing strategies. The implementation of adaptive scaling mechanisms within H-STREAM enables the seamless distribution and recovery of stream processing applications across multi-node and multi-machine environments, ensuring optimal performance and minimizing data loss in case of failures. The effectiveness of H-STREAM has been evaluated through both simulated scenarios and real-world applications of managing smart energy data. The framework's open-source availability, along with its platform-independent design, allows for the seamless integration of new stream processing operators and external data management systems, as well as deployment on a variety of distributed platforms. The experimental results obtained from the evaluation of H-STREAM have shown significant scalability and performance benefits, particularly in complex decision-making processes involving energy management and optimization. The output parameters obtained from the evaluation of H-STREAM have also demonstrated high accuracy and relevance in addressing real-world energy management challenges, such as predicting energy consumption, identifying energy efficiency opportunities, and streamlining energy-curtailment management. The current limitations of H-STREAM have also been identified and proposed for future improvement, offering opportunities for further research and development in the area of stream-based data and analytics management. The application of H-STREAM has also led to the identification of additional research potential in the areas of query execution, external data management, decision-making, and other related topics, providing a comprehensive understanding of the current state of the art in the context of the proposed research framework. In a specific type of particle collisions that involve t or b quarks, we investigate the production of heavier particles that lie beyond the boundaries of a predefined phase space region. This collision process is unique because it cannot be described solely by the production of known intermediate particles, such as gluons or heavy bosons. Instead, the production amplitude cancels out when the collision energy falls within a particular phase space region. This unique property leads to a situation in which the total amplitude approaches zero within that region. We now provide two new case studies that demonstrate this phenomenon. First, we consider the collision of two gluons resulting in t and b quarks, where one of the gluons plays a crucial role in satisfying momentum conservation. We show that if the momentum of one of the gluons lies within a specific phase space region, the total amplitude cancels out. Second, we consider a collision involving a heavy fundamental boson and gluons, where one of the gluons plays a crucial role in satisfying momentum conservation. We show that if the momentum of one of the gluons lies within a specific phase space region, the total amplitude cancels out. Both cases share a common feature, as the total amplitude in both processes can be described by a term involving a propagator. This term would otherwise contribute to a process involving the production of two gluons at a specific energy level in the standard model, but this contribution is eliminated in the specific energy phase space in question. This cancellation of terms at a specific energy level could potentially be observed in experiments searching for rare processes involving t or b quarks, such as the production of four bosons or more rare processes such as those involving the production of four gluons or five or more gluons. These processes can be searched for at the Large Hadron Collider, which has recently started a new program to explore these types of processes. We propose an alternative approach that offers more straightforward insights into the discourse and editing processes at work within the academic community. We examined a representative dataset of over 3700 conferences and 1500 journals from the Computer Science domain, tracking the relationship between bibliometric measures and the quality of resulting research. Our analysis showed that, in contrast to citation metrics, our new approach has the advantage of offering clear, consistent, and comparable results across various types of academic publications, providing valuable insights through accessible and comprehensive visualizations. Furthermore, this new approach has the potential to be used more frequently, such as during strategic decision-making in venue selection, in both internal and external editing processes. We believe that, with the rise of large-scale digital repositories and computational power, this new approach has the potential to revolutionize academic communication. Additionally, we offer suggestions for how to best utilize the new approach, as well as the associated challenges and limitations. This entails verifying that neural network-based solutions meet specified validation criteria, which are connected and conform to higher-level policy requirements. Clustering is a crucial technique used for data analysis in numerous fields. In this paper, we address the issue of overlapping clusters, as hard partitions fail to effectively capture the complexity of data. Overlapping groups allow for the capture of multiple information sources and handle missing data. From a theoretical standpoint, we develop a functorial overlapping clustering method, building on existing hard partitioning approaches. Our proposed functor can be applied in various ways, each of which corresponds to a traditional clustering method when the overlap is disregarded. To evaluate the quality of overlaps, we introduce functors that measure overlap magnitude and compare our method's performance to state-of-the-art methods using simulated data, demonstrating its effectiveness. Moreover, functorial overlapping clustering enables the derivation of an unsupervised evaluation metric, similar to the Consensus Index. This new index assesses the level of agreement among different clustering runs, providing a data-driven approach to setting the level of overlap. Our approach is demonstrated through application to breast cancer expression data, offering novel insights into the data. Additionally, we provide pre-trained functorial clustering models for widespread use. They can be downloaded from https://github.com/alexkamber/functorial-clustering. \medskip E. Kamber, E. The atmospheric science and engineering fields have significantly benefited from understanding turbulent inertial waves, yet researchers still debate the underlying frequency spectrum of these waves. A convergent point has been lacking due to conflicting theories and models. We present numerical calculations that provide the first concrete evidence for the high-frequency end of the Kolmogorov spectrum as per the theory first introduced by Zakharov and Kolmogorov. The $-5/3$ frequency slope has been observed in our simulations, which were carried out with a simplified model of homogeneous and isotropic turbulent inertial waves. We observed this spectrum in three distinct cases of total energy levels, which also revealed the transition to chaotic behavior. Our results, in turn, facilitate a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between infrared and ultraviolet frequency scales of inertial wave chaos. These results also lead to a crucial assumption for future statistical models in this field. The observed spectrum is resistant to the effects of chaos. Our work has further shown that using only the high-frequency behavior of incompressible fluid dynamics could already predict useful and accurate results in the limit of weak dissipation. This approach has also enabled a numerical estimation of how many simulation results are required to confidently assess dissipation in such systems. Specifically, our experiments have shown that at least six significant decimal places must be considered in simulation parameters to ensure and verify dissipation. The observed high-frequency behavior has further allowed us to estimate that for relevant atmospheric conditions, the higher frequency end of the $-5/3$ frequency spectrum is located at a frequency of approximately $10^^-8$ Hz. Our results also have further shown that using only the high-frequency behavior of in decomposition is sufficient to accurately model and predict the overall behavior of the system. Our and work has also demonstrated that even in the limit of weak dissipation, the observed high-frequency behavior is not affected the stability of the low-frequency dynamics. Our numerical results also have further revealed a significant amount of statistical sample required to reliably estimate several relevant parameters and physical processes that express themselves through high-frequency. Specifically, our experiments have shown that at least sixty-five significant decimal places must be considered in the statistical sample in order to accurately estimate these parameters and processes. Our work has also further shown an efficient way to implement and run such numerical experiments and simulations in order to reduce the computational requirements.
