A single layer of Graphene was surgically inserted into the center of a C60 fullerene molecule surrounded by six layers of carbon atoms. Initially, the system was equilibrated at 300 K and 1 atm to study its heat capacity and entropy in relation to the third law of thermodynamics. Furthermore, an external electric field was applied to the system to investigate how the heat capacity and entropy are affected, and then an examination was conducted to establish the time it takes for the system to reach complete thermodynamic equilibrium when subjected to different heating and cooling protocols. All simulations were based on classical mechanics and implemented using the NVE and NVE-VV algorithms. Following these results, an assessment was made as to whether it is feasible to achieve a reversible Carnot engine using the system of fullerene molecules. Nevertheless, due to the rapid growth of entropy during the simulation, it was found impossible to attain a reversible cycle. Consequently, additional modifications to the system were considered with a view to studying the Carnot cycle. Nonetheless, it was also recognized that electrical manipulation of single Graphene molecules holds potential for realizing a reversible Carnot engine despite the significant challenges that need to be overcome. All simulations were performed using the Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics program, and the data analysis was conducted using the Python programming language along with its relevant scientific libraries. Lastly, it is anticipated that further research into the electrical manipulation of single Graphene molecules may yield more satisfactory results in the future. A virtually rendered human figure can be represented as a combination of its skeleton, articulation, and surface details. Current methods that attempt to render realistic avatars often separate these components into individual images and employ distinct techniques to account for pose changes and detailed feature variations. However, this two-stage approach can be impractical for applications involving multiple users, as it necessitates the creation and alignment of numerous detailed images from various perspectives. In this context, we introduce a novel method, referred to as Articulated Neural Representation (ANR), that seamlessly integrates skeleton, articulation, and surface details into a single image. Our approach relies on a neural rendering framework and allows the creation of realistic avatars through a simplified process involving a single image and pose-embedded 3D templates. Additionally, ANR enables the generation of multiple views from a single image and unlocks novel applications, such as real-time rendering of multiple views from a single image. Our avatar rendering method produces high-quality results, outperforming existing techniques in both visual fidelity and articulation details, as demonstrated by our experiments. Furthermore, our analysis confirms the feasibility of creating ANR from real images without ground truth skeleton information, articulation, or surface details. Our work specifically explores applications in social media, reenacting photos with support for multiple view generation and dynamic overlays for interactive content creation. There are distinct approaches taken by humans and machines when interpreting images. While humans consider images in relation to their broader context, computers rely on larger datasets to learn patterns. This difference in perspective becomes apparent when images undergo significant alterations, which are perceived differently by humans and machines. To explore this phenomenon further, we developed the IntImage dataset, comprising 630 images along with corresponding annotations, used in a study that evaluated how strongly these images are associated with various labels across five diverse image classification tasks. Our investigation revealed that heavily modified images are categorized by humans in a more nuanced manner based on specific attributes, whereas computers tend to categorize them more conservatively, closely related to the image's original label. The IntImage dataset has been made publicly available to facilitate future research into this phenomenon. The study's findings hold broader implications for understanding image classification, as well as the integration of human and mechanical image analysis. The dataset can be accessed at https://intimage.github.io/. The associated code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/gitavlshay/IntImage. The image data can be downloaded from https://drive.google.com/file/d/1h0o1k. The dataset's integrity can be verified using the hash code 2021a4d2c. To build on this, our study centers around pre-trained language models that can perform tasks without needing to be specifically trained on each task. To achieve this, we developed an innovative method, assembling and structuring educational tasks in a standard format to optimize the performance of these models. This, in turn, enables us to produce enhanced models by fine-tuning them using a dataset composed of various task configurations. The outcome of our method was evident in the notable improvement of ZILO models, which showed a 6.8% increase in average EM score and a 7.2% increase in average F1 score after being meta-tuned using a dataset comprised of 7 diverse math datasets, as well as two smaller English subject datasets where our model outperformed GPT3 in zero-shot setup. Additionally, we successfully extended our method to multiple answer types and developed an evaluation dataset to facilitate further research in this area. The entire process, from task assembly to model meta-tuning, was conducted in an automated manner, which we refer to as AutoAssembly. Our study's findings have implications for how we design and interpret educational datasets, giving rise to a broader set of questions about dataset configuration and its impact on model performance and transferability. The proposed method enables us to produce enhanced models by fine-tuning them using a dataset composed of multiple task configurations, which in turn allows for better transferability to other task configurations, which we refer to as Configurable Transferability. This method holds promise for enhancing the performance of language models, which in turn has the potential to improve educational outcomes when used as an additional resource. The proposed dataset allows for better understanding of how educational datasets are constructed, which in turn has the potential to improve the design of future educational datasets. Lastly, we propose a new paradigm, Assembled and Configurable Knowledge Distillation, which involves training several models on various task configurations, which in turn enables better transferability to other task configurations, which in turn enables better educational outcomes when used as an additional resource. The method holds promise for further research and we expect to see significant advancements in the future. The proposed method is compatible with few-shot learning as well and we expect to see notable improvements there as well. We have developed an interactive web-based tool, known as "High-z Sudoku," for determining redshift confidence through time-frequency correlations in millimetric spectral data. The code is hosted at https://redshift-sudoku.github.io/. By visualizing correlations, users can infer redshifts, which is particularly advantageous since this approach doesn't depend on predicting galaxy spectra. We demonstrate the effectiveness of High-z Sudoku by applying it to simulated spectra with diverse features and then use it to analyze redshifts in a subset of 10 sources from the REDCOBS database with complex millimetric spectra. Based on this analysis, we estimate that approximately 53% of sources in the REDCOBS database have reliable redshifts via High-z Sudoku. We anticipate that high-resolution millimetric observations will become increasingly sensitive to redshifted molecular, 21 cm H.I., and dust kinetic temperature signatures, which can serve as strong indicators of redshift even in the absence of detectable millimetric continuum or line signals. High-z Sudoku is poised to take full advantage of this trend by providing an adaptive, user-driven means to leverage time-frequency correlations in redshift searches. We envision applying this tool in the analysis of future large millimetric surveys, which could rely on High-z Sudoku to infer redshifts for a substantial fraction of their targets. We also anticipate incorporating machine learning algorithms that utilize the graph-generated features to further boost the performance of redshift identification. Finally, High-z Sudoku can be adapted to analyze millimetric and submillimetric data in various observational contexts including those targeting submm-bright galaxies, quasars, or star-forming galaxies with extensive dust emission. We anticipate this tool being particularly useful in the analysis of future large surveys for near-infrared millimetric redshifts in the COASTAL3D, ALMA CO(3-2) and WISE, ALMA GOODS-ALMA 4D databases, which could enhance the detection of the cosmic recombination emission, study the alignment between galaxies and black holes, analyze near-infrared millimetric spectra and identify galaxies with dust kinetic temperature anomalies. High-z Sudoku is open-source, allowing the community to access the source code at https://github.com/Github-3999/Redshift-Sudoku. Recent breakthroughs in large language models have led to significant advancements in understanding natural language, but they are still far from being truly knowledgeable interpreters of language, a goal first proposed by Quine in 1960. Unlike them, current models don't consider themselves ignorant of language and aren't motivated to learn more. To address this, we developed a naturalized interpreter that can learn without prior knowledge and motivate it to acquire new knowledge as needed. Our model performs well in answering questions with minimal human supervision and outperforms its non-naturalized counterpart. For the Electron-Ion Collider's upcoming phase, precise measurements of heavy quark nuclei will depend on positive charge particle tracking. A proposed silicon tracker based on a point-like sensor concept could meet this project's requirements. This concept was tested using a dedicated prototype sensor called a SICLIDE pixel sensor, designed to minimize its detection volume and utilize low-radiation technology to ensure it functions optimally in the EIC's beam test environment. Thorough research and testing of this sensor's capabilities have been conducted, including automated functional, radiation, and backscattering analysis. Furthermore, a framework for evaluating electron hit patterns and finding hit clusters has been established using a dedicated hit-finding algorithm, designed to meet the tracker's hit-resolution requirements. Consequently, this phase of development has confirmed the compatibility of this advanced technology sensor with the EIC's requirements, paving the way for its integration into the Electron-Ion Collider. A detailed description of this process and these results is provided in this presentation, including detailed background information on the EIC's sensor requirements, the SICLIDE sensor's characteristics, the testing procedures, and the results of the compatibility analysis. A SICLIDE sensor development roadmap that will take it to the next stage of development, including a proposed integration into the EIC, is also outlined. This integration will involve incorporating the sensor into a so-called "micro-mechanical" frame by the EIC, as part of a larger strip tracker that will be developed in two stages, first by ORNL and then by BNL. A similar development roadmap has been proposed for another silicon detector developed at Fermilab, as part of LHeC's future LHCC program. A summary of these two development roads and their integration into the EIC has been provided by the EIC's Detector Development for the 2022-2029 period in reports by NSF and DOE, as of their 2022 updates. A planned integration into the FCC-ee has also been proposed by the FCC-ee LHeC, as of its 2020 update. A similar integration into the HL-LHC by the FCC-ee, as of its 2020 update, was proposed until it was replaced by the FCC-ee by the FCC hadron collider in the 2022 updates of the FCC and LHeC reports respectively. Our analysis of the NGC 5253 dwarf galaxy, observed with ALMA with an exceptionally high spatial resolution, demonstrates the effectiveness of observing star-forming regions at very low metal levels using the H30$\alpha$ radiospin emission. NGC 5253, at a low metal content of 0.00001 solar masses ratio, lacks massive star formations above a mass limit of approximately 12 solar masses. However, fine-scale observations of H30$\alpha$ emissions reveal the existence of 8-12 solar mass star formations. This implies that these could be the initial high mass star formations before becoming more massive due to metal accumulation from previous star explosions. A comparison with the galaxy M33 shows NGC 5253 has about 1000 times fewer 8-12 solar mass star formations. Observations of emission spectra in both NGC 5253 and M33 reveal the presence of a red-shifted emission peak at approximately 36 km/s in NGC5253 and at approximately 12 km/s in M33, suggesting the red-shifted peak may be an indicator of emerging star formations in NGC5253. A similar role as Lyman-$\alpha$ emission in the process of low metal galaxy stellar genesis is also proposed. A potential alternative is that the red-shifted peak at approximately 36 km/s in NGC5253 may be an indicator of a super nova remnant. A longer observation period is required to confirm the nature of NGC5253's red-shifted emission. A similar observation method could be effective in other galaxies with low metal content such as Sagittarius A-North. Reinforcement learning agents are susceptible to various types of risk, and optimal policies often involve a trade-off between return and expected loss. Traditional measures of Bellman bias interpret variance or expected loss, but these one-dimensional assessments have limitations, as variance does not consistently capture expected loss, and both do not evaluate risk in the tail. To address these limitations, we introduce a multi-dimensional concept of Bellman risk and investigate its structural properties. We also develop a novel, scalable risk management approach based on this risk measure, which allows us to find the most effective parameter settings for maximizing returns while minimizing expected loss. Our method does not require knowing the distribution of losses and can handle cases where expected loss does not exist. We demonstrate the performance of our approach in synthetic and real-world scenarios, and show that using our method to model variance or expected loss leads to worse outcomes compared to optimized policies. Additionally, our results reveal that variance often overestimates expected loss and that both measures underestimate risk in certain cases. Our work lays the foundation for applying statistical tools from extreme value theory to the study of Bellman risk. We hope that our research promotes further understanding and development of risk management strategies for reinforcement learning agents. We release our code at https://github.com/krindgus/profound-bellman-risk.

Research into DL models that can handle both speech and text through multilingual approaches has gained less attention, particularly in regards to teacher-data availability. We explore this gap by implementing a symmetrical, adversarial training method that improves model performance on both speech and text tasks. Our study shows that training our model with adversarial examples generated by an aggressive teacher results in better performance on Wav2Text, LSMT, Librispeech, and STS datasets compared to other training methods, suggesting that data availability doesn't impact the effectiveness of our training approach. Moreover, our model performs better when the teacher's goal is to mislead the model compared to when the teacher's goal is to provide accurate information. These counterintuitive results suggest that overfitting can actually enhance learning in certain contexts and that delving into the adversarial robustness of education programs could lead to breakthroughs in the field. Ultimately, we demonstrate that training our model to be more robust against adversarial examples by using a variety of gradient-based methods, such as PGD and FGSM, leads to improved speech recognition performance. However, we do find that certain methods can make the model perform worse and overfit more severely. We attribute this mixed bag of results to the intricate dynamics of model education, which is particularly evident in the case of text data. Our work highlights the significance of carefully designing educational programs, which in turn necessitates a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics of model learning. It also sheds light on the potential for leveraging adversarial training techniques to drive learning outcomes in certain contexts. To address the issue of incomplete data in medical studies, we employ the e-value, a measure of incomplete data influence, and develop a Bayesian version for unbiased or biased missing data scenarios. This Bayesian e-value is calculated as the ratio of two posterior odds, comparing alternative to base hypotheses. In this context, the base hypothesis involves assuming missing outcome data to be zero, while the alternative hypothesis posits the opposite. The missing data odds ratio is estimated in two common cases – when outcomes are binary and when they are continuous and normally distributed. The proposed Bayesian e-value is illustrated through its application in two hypothetical studies and demonstrates a high degree of correspondence with its frequentist counterpart. The proliferation of cryptocurrency use has been accompanied by concerns regarding its privacy. As a practical means of measuring privacy, researchers have employed cryptocurrency transaction graph analysis to quantify anonymity. A notable study in 2012 assessed misuses of the Tor anonymization tool by analyzing it in real-world instances; our research undertakes a similar examination; our research focuses on Python, as code misuses often lead to privacy breaches, and we aim to identify misuses observed in real-world Python cryptocurrency code. To achieve this goal, we created a comprehensive dataset consisting of 27 popular Python libraries used in cryptocurrency development and tested 378 unique code examples for misuses, also drawing inspiration from existing studies on Tor misuses. Our analysis reveals that the following misuses prevail: Unnecessary data collection, inadequate data processing, unencrypted sensitive data, insecure password storage, network exploitation, malicious scripts, insecure HTTP requests, unencrypted sensitive data, insecure FTP requests, malicious Tor usage, unencrypted sensitive data, malicious Twitter usage, and excessive data transmission. A thorough discussion of our results enables developers to comprehend and address privacy breaches related to popular Python cryptocurrency usage, thereby enhancing anonymity in cryptocurrency transactions. Additionally, we provide developers with actionable guidelines to prevent such misuses in their own work. Our research results have potential implications for other anonymization tools and tangible software products, and can also expand to other programming languages by adapting our research approach. A crucial outcome of our research is that, beyond misuses, we can also promote responsible usage of sensitive data when utilizing cryptocurrency services. Moreover, our research opens up an opportunity for a more extensive investigation into coding best practices for anonymity tools.

Valuable urban infrastructure relies heavily on unmarked vehicles, which are crucial for a range of activities including emergency response, unlicensed rideshare services, bike and bike-sharing systems, and food delivery. Comprehending the scale and intricacies of unmarked traffic is vital for urban planners, as it affects factors like congestion, city layout design, and environmental issues. However, due to their lack of visual identification, unmarked vehicles often go undetected in traditional traffic counting methods, which have led to significant gaps in our understanding of their behavior. To bridge this knowledge gap, we developed WORTH, a pioneering system that combines machine learning and data from crowd-sourced platforms to automatically identify unmarked vehicles in urban settings. By using a large dataset of 55,875 geolocated vehicle trips, which includes over 14,000 instances of unmarked vehicles, WORTH's model achieves an impressive accuracy of reconstructing the path of unmarked vehicles. Furthermore, our city-wide analysis demonstrates that unmarked vehicles make up approximately 16.2% of all vehicles and travel a total distance of about 690 kilometers per day. With WORTH's data-driven approach, urban researchers can gain a more informed understanding of the impact of unmarked vehicles. WORTH's source code is available for the public to replicate and improve. Additionally, we observed that the emergence of unmarked vehicles is not a modern phenomenon but rather a gradual transformation from marked to unmarked vehicles. Specifically, our data shows that 16.7% of cars, 13.2% of trucks, and 19.8% of vans eventually lose their marks over time. Importantly, our analysis reveals that the majority of these marked vehicles tend to change their status during mid-day hours, which implies that they may be engaged in ride-sharing or other forms of commercial activities. Therefore, it appears that the shift from marked to unmarked vehicles could be largely attributed to the proliferation of sharing economies. With WORTH's objective fact-based findings, urban policymakers can effectively address this by considering sharing-related activities in urban infrastructure planning, city layout design, and environmental programs, rather than viewing them as regular private vehicles. WORTH's results can also guide cities to establish appropriate regulations for these services, which in turn can ensure that the benefits of urban mobility are made accessible to all. Ultimately, our analysis confirms that urban mobility is heavily influenced by the sharing economy, which must be acknowledged and leveraged by city planners. The task of part-of-speech tagging historical texts is particularly challenging,
given their linguistic differences and limited annotation. Furthermore, the
limited availability of training data in historical dialects poses an additional
obstacle. Existing predictive models can fall short when encountering out-of-
 vocabulary words or words without part-of-speech annotations in parallel
corpora. A novel approach to addressing these challenges is presented, based on
utilizing sequences of tokens and parts of speech to predict portions of the
sequence. This technique is set-valued, allowing it to generate a set of likely
part-of-speech sequences, rather than solely predicting an optimal sequence.
Alongside this optimization, a contribution is made to the field by using
cross-entropy to evaluate set-valued forecasting models, despite current state-
of-the-art evaluations relying on mean-average-preCISION measures. Through
experiments using annotated books from various collections, the proposed
approach demonstrates a notable improvement in handling unknown words and
the prediction of part-of-speech sequences. Notably, the proposed model outperforms
existing state-of-the-art models in predicting part-of-speech sequences for
words appearing five or fewer times in two collections. When asked to generate
a single part-of-speech sequence, the proposed model performs competitively,
yielding a performance comparable to the best existing model. Furthermore, the
proposed approach shows potential in handling cross-parallel corpus alignment,
a challenge that existing models have struggled with. Overall, the proposed
approach demonstrates a notable improvement in part-of-speech sequence
prediction and the reliance on out-of-vocabulary words, while the proposed
evaluation method has the potential to broaden the scope of existing
evaluations. Future work involves the application of the proposed technique
to translate historical texts in parallel corpora. The proposed technique is
available for further research at github.com/slalexi/set-valued-forecasting.

Through numerical analysis using a superconducting quantum circuit as a test case, we compute the theoretical limits of the parameter ranges for the concealed inverses protocol and associated phase modulation schemes required to achieve substantial error reduction. The task of estimating a matrix's inverse from impaired linear measurements is a fundamental, yet challenging issue in mathematics. This problem has been studied extensively under the assumption that measurements are influenced by a limited, stationary noise process. To address this problem, a comprehensive theoretical framework for determining the inverse's estimation accuracy is needed. However, existing theories only apply to a limited range of noise conditions, making the general case increasingly difficult to solve. Furthermore, as the size of the matrix increases, the number of necessary measurements grows rapidly, leading to increasingly expensive data collection needs. This paper introduces a novel approach that achieves accurate estimation even in situations where existing methods fail, given the right noisy measurements. This approach is then used to derive a universal criterion for estimating a matrix's inverse under any stationary noise condition, assuming a sufficient level of measurements is collected. This criterion is based on the stability of an operator that'switches' between matrix components, providing a universal metric for estimation accuracy. This approach is expanded to address the estimation of a matrix's inverse through a limited set of non-parametric observations. Although the general case remains difficult to solve, our approach allows the quality of noisy linear measurements to be accurately assessed through a universal operator, leading to improved estimation accuracy and reduced data collection costs in scenarios where the size of the matrix increases. Finally, related results are presented for the estimation of a low-rank matrix or a function's inverse. Additional research investigates the application of our method to the estimation of a matrix's inverse based on a limited set of data. This research highlights the approach's practical utility in addressing real-world challenges, such as the estimation of a camera's parameters in computer vision. Moreover, our approach's theoretical limitations have significant implications for the development of advanced machine learning and image reconstruction techniques. This research can potentially inspire breakthroughs in related areas, including the estimation of a matrix's inverse or a function's inverse, which may have far-reaching applications in physics and related fields. This research is complemented by a series of numerical studies that demonstrate the approach's efficiency and effectiveness, highlighting its potential to address a range of applicable problems, including the estimation of a matrix's inverse or a function's inverse. To showcase the method's applicability, numerical studies were conducted in various fields. For example, the approach was tested in the estimation of a matrix's inverse or a function's inverse in the context of the LOFAR planetary radio astronomy system. This research contributes to the development of a theoretical framework for the estimation of a matrix's inverse or a function's inverse

We define the compact Hilbert function of M as the collection of dimensions of these modules,
and the compact Hilbert polynomial when the dimensions are finite.
This study explores properties of the compact Hilbert polynomial and demonstrates
that for F-regular local rings, the polynomial's leading coefficient aligns with the ring's
regularity in the sense of Hartshorne-Lichtenbaum.
Additionally, if the polynomial's degree equals 1, the ring satisfies a specific condition.
This work also identifies characteristics of F-regularity through the study of the compact Hilbert
polynomial, and provides examples by considering power series over F-regular bases of length 2. 
Furthermore, if R has a regular residual ring, a polynomial's leading coefficient aligns
with the ring's expected regularity, and we define another invariant that corrects for irregularity. 
Lastly, examples demonstrate that neither the degree nor the leading coefficient necessarily
equal those of the ring's Hilbert function. 
This study also examines semilocal cases and implies results for local rings that are universally
Cohen-Macaulay. 
It remains unknown whether universally Cohen-Macaulay rings have a degree 1 compact Hilbert polynomial. 
Lastly, we provide an illustration of how some results can be applied to particular types of rings. 
One type includes the study of the compact Hilbert polynomial of modules on toric rings, which may have
utility for approaches in commutative algebra, such as the study of the compact Hilbert polynomial as a tool. 
In the process, we derive a result that describes a polynomial's degree in terms of the degrees of its
irreducible factors, which may have broader applications. 
This work is primarily conducted in the context of Noetherian rings, but some results extend to more general ring types. 
Specifically, in the context of modules over commutative rings, some results remain valid for rings without assumptions of $R_0$ or Noetherian conditions.

Consider a graph $G$ and a mapping that assigns colors to its edges, denoted as $f: E(G) \to \mathbb{R}$, such that adjacent edges receive different colors. For a graph $G$ with edge coloring $f$, an edge sub-decomposition of $G$ with respect to a vertex subset $S$ is defined as follows: given $G$ and $S$, find a subset $\mathcal{H}$ of $G$'s edge sub-graphs such that: (i) each edge in $G$ belongs to at most one edge in $\mathcal{H}$, (ii) edges in $\mathcal{H}$ share endpoints only if they are adjacent in $G$, and (iii) for an edge $e$ in $\mathcal{H}$, if both its endpoints are in $S$, then $e$ has different color from the edge incident to it in $\mathcal{H}$. Such a sub-decomposition is said to exist in $G$ for $S$ when the conditions above are met, and is termed as $S$-edge sub-decomposition or $S$-edge-tinting in $G$ or bold-$(G,S)$-edge-tinting. We investigate the existence of such a sub-decomposition for bipartite graphs of high expansion, particularly for complete bipartite graphs in this work, and derive a condition on the smaller of the two bipartite set's cardinality for them to possess the property that every subset of vertices has an edge sub-decomposition in the form of a complete bipartite graph. Additionally, in the context of complete graphs, we investigate the existence of such a sub-decomposition for all possible subset of vertices. Finally, in the context of graphs of diameter at most $2$, we investigate the existence of such a sub-decomposition for all possible subset of vertices. Detecting COVID-19 from computed tomography scans is crucial for managing patients. Although capsule networks offer superior representation capabilities, their application in detecting COVID-19 from CT images has not been extensively explored. This study introduces a two-stage capsule network model, specifically designed for handling sequences of CT images, with each stage utilizing a time-distributed capsule dynamic neural network to extract information from patches within the images. The first stage identifies healthy cases, while the second distinguishes between healthy and infected cases. Evaluating the model on a large dataset yielded a high detection accuracy of 0.9401, along with excellent routine assessment metrics. Moreover, the study investigated how different capsule network architecture components affect performance, revealing improved results when utilizing multiple capsules and Gru capsules, as well as a beneficial trade-off between detection performance and computational cost. This research provides valuable insights for guiding the design of capsule networks for sequences and highlights their vast potential for medical image analysis. The research also emphasizes the significance of accurately labeling imaging data for analysis tasks. A revolutionary shift is occurring in how we interact with space, driven by changing economic and technological landscapes. Initially, space technology focused on overcoming physical limitations, but now the escalating use of services and systems in low-earth orbit requires efficient management of available resources. The primary challenge is utilizing space effectively by minimizing the impact of structural components such as spacecraft and launching vehicles. This paper examines space utilization as an extension of area optimization and classifies problems within this context, before presenting solutions for two core issues: minimizing debris and launching multiple missions simultaneously. The proposed approach involves an algorithm based on a dynamic linear programming problem with moving constraints, whose basins of attraction can be identified using a geometric method. The solutions for these problems not only offer mathematical validation but also serve as a foundation for developing more complex algorithms and tackling more complex space utilization problems in the future. The approaches presented have already proven applicable in various real-world scenarios. Mesh coarsening is a process that simplifies a fine mesh while maintaining its topology, although it has limitations as it's often unsuitable for use alone due to loss of detail. Mesh refinement, on the other hand, is a process that adds detail to a coarse mesh, but it can be problematic as it may generate irregular results, especially in complex areas. In this paper, a novel method for creating high-order coarse meshes directly from CAD models is presented. By utilizing the geometry of the design and linear optimization techniques to maximize a function with integer coefficients, a mesh with desirable topological properties and precise boundary alignment can be produced. To further enhance the mesh's quality, a category-theoretic algorithm is applied to create quadrilateral shapes that meet specific criteria. The resulting mesh can then be used as a starting point for analysis or optimization, with the option to refine it using standard methods. The proposed approach is supported by theoretical analysis and numerical experiments. The results demonstrate that this method produces meshes with high-quality properties such as small L2 errors, minimal Hobbs ratios, and optimal angle distributions. The method's performance is tested using various CAD models and demanding numerical scenarios like Navier-Stokes simulations. The study shows that these meshes allow for stable solutions and significant improvements in computational efficiency compared to fine meshes, with minimal impact on accuracy. The method's potential applications and future developments are also explored. The method's implementation can be found at github.com/czhi-wang/coarse-mesh-generation. Mind maps, used for organizing information and concepts, have long been an effective tool. A particular type of mind map, known as a concept map, has gained popularity among language learners and individuals seeking to expand their vocabulary. Although existing resources, such as online flashcards, have sought to fill this need, they are often marred by shortcomings like complicated navigation and a lack of user involvement. To address this gap, we introduce the LitMind Lexicon (LLL), a user-driven web dictionary that empowers users to participate in maintaining a comprehensive, searchable dictionary of English words and their definitions. The LLL facilitates user contribution and is open-source, allowing users to adapt and improve the platform as they see fit. The LLL is available at https://litmind.net. The source code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/litmind-lexicon. The data used to develop the LLL can be accessed through https://dx.dryzius.github.io/litmind-ensemble/. The LLL is licensed under a GNU General Public License, allowing users to modify it for their needs. The platform is primarily supported through donations, with further details available at https://donate.litmind.net. The LLL is designed to be translated into multiple languages, with users encouraged to submit translations at https://form.litmind.net. The development of the LLL was facilitated by a community of volunteer translators and validators, demonstrating the power of collaborative development and translation. The platform is backed by an extensive ensemble of machine learning models, trained on diverse datasets, including WordNet, Wiktionary, and Wikipedia's database. The LLL's user interface is optimized for accessibility and usability, with a mobile-friendly design and passing high standards for accessibility in the US. The user experience is further enhanced by a range of features, including definition pop-ups, a typing delay, a search auto-completer, and user tracking. The LLL is headquartered in Berlin, Germany, with its development guided by the principles of Software as a Service (SaaS) and Open Source Software. In various contexts, contextual machine learning is gaining traction. Particular emphasis is placed on recommended systems (SL), a subclass of contextual SL, due to their vast potential for positive impact in people's daily lives. Unlike conventional approaches, systems without knowledge of their own models face challenges in providing transparent explanations to users, which hinders their ability to learn and improve in the long run. A breakthrough called LIME-RS has addressed this challenge by creating understandable explanations for recommended systems through a machine-learning-based approach. However, this method does not guarantee explanations that align with user perspectives on relevance for a given recommendation. Research has shown that users consider multiple factors, including diversity, when evaluating relevance, which is not currently accounted for in LIME-RS. In response, our study focuses on interpreting LIME-RS interpretations through a diversity-compliance optimization method. A diversity-related attribute is identified, and an optimization problem is formulated to ensure improved stability in LIME-RS interpretations by capping feature-weight variability. When tested using the most popular recommendation datasets, results demonstrate that our method enhances long-term compliance and stability of LIME-RS interpretations by over 119% across all datasets. We have also shown that a trained policy from our method boosts its overall performance by 7.64% and 9.23% in terms of accuracy and average discount, respectively, when applied to a reinforcement learning agent as opposed to a non-optimized policy. Research reveals that LIME-RS interpretations do not consistently reflect diversity as a key factor for relevance in recommended systems. However, our method effectively enhances the representativeness of LIME-RS interpretations by capping feature-weight variability, thus ensuring improved compliance and stability. We have also found that a LIME-RS-based reinforcement learning agent performs better on average when guided by a diversified and stabilized interpretation as opposed to an unsystematic and less-reliable one. Research highlights the need for systems without model knowledge of their own to be made transparent through the utilization of machine-learning-based methods, such as LIME, particularly in recommended systems. In order to enhance the potential for positive impact in people's daily lives, our method effectively addresses the long-term compliance and stability challenges in LIME-RS interpretations. A comparison of our method, denoted as LiDGeT, and existing diversity-based LIME-RS methods reveals that our approach surpasses others, including multi-objective LIME-RS, in achieving increased compliance and stability by over 63% and 116.64% respectively. Quantum device development relies heavily on the principles of quantum tunneling and the principles of quantum confinement. One key technology in this area is quantum tunneling-based electron emission, which serves as a crucial component for various quantum computer and light-emitting diode-based technologies. Researchers have made significant progress in understanding and improving this phenomenon, although managing it remains challenging due to surface charges. This issue can be addressed through the use of heterojunctions, which consist of different materials with varying band gaps. One such design, near-surface InAs/AlInAs quantum wells, shows great potential, but poses a challenge due to its thinness. This study focuses on the potential issues associated with surface charges in these very thin quantum wells, and proposes management techniques utilizing the Fermi level fixation method. This technique involves introducing a metal gate without a Schottky barrier to control the electrostatic forces near the surface. Researchers employed state-of-the-art first-principles band structure calculations to simulate the electronic properties of these near-surface quantum wells, and to investigate the effectiveness of the metal gate in managing surface charges. They compared the electronic properties of two designs: one with an InAs/AlInAs quantum well, and another with an InAs/AlAs quantum well. The simulations showed that the metal gate plays a crucial role in improving emission times, and that the electronic properties of the two designs can be modified with the metal gate. However, the simulations revealed that the metal gate fails to manage surface charges in the InAs/AlInAs quantum well, while it is successful in managing surface charges in the InAs/AlAs quantum well. Researchers demonstrated the emission times of the two designs can be improved with the metal gate, and that the metal gate can be used to improve the device's performance by shifting the energy overlap between the two materials. This research offers a crucial perspective on the development of quantum device technologies based on tunneling and confinement principles. It provides important design guidelines for improving near-surface InAs/AlInAs quantum wells, and proposes a management technique for these designs with potential for application in various quantum computer and light-emitting diode-based technologies. The technique, Fermi level fixation, is a general approach that can be applied to manage surface charges in thin quantum wells, and is a valuable tool for designers. The study also focuses on the development of quantum devices that utilize the tunneling and confinement principles, and is a crucial contribution to this field. To achieve resilient learning, clients typically send standardized queries to the server, regardless of the data they're interested in. However, if clients could specify relevant information in their queries, the server could process and return more tailored results, potentially improving overall performance. Regional queries have shown potential in this area, but the key lies in understanding when utilizing them yields superior results. Our investigation delves into this very question, with a focus on two key factors: the minimum required regional queries for robust generalization, and the optimal distribution of such queries. Through both theoretical analysis and empirical verification, our results suggest that regional queries offer advantages, but only under specific conditions, namely when clients have limited capacity and clients' regional labels align with the true data clusters. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that in cases where regional queries hold value, employing them across all clients leads to superior generalization compared to using standardized queries. These findings illuminate the key assumptions underlying regional query-based methods for resilient learning and highlight the complexities involved in integrating such queries into existing robust federated learning frameworks. Measurements of single-electron tunneling between a quantum point and a superconducting island are sensitive to the island's state, which can be monitored by the charge and the temperature of the island. Initially, the focus is on the normal skin depth $\lambda_{\mathrm{N}}$ that determines the island's temperature and charge distributions, leading to two scenarios: tunneling electrons can originate from within the bulk or from a layer close to the island. As the temperature increases, the island's behavior shifts from a high-temperature regime with multiple tunneling sites to a low-temperature regime with a single tunneling site, located very close to the island, and corresponding to a specific characteristic energy. However, this energy can deviate from the expected dependence on the island's size when the bulk is the primary source of tunneling electrons due to the influence of the Cox pairs' correlations. Furthermore, the interaction between the island and its surroundings, particularly with a nearby Cox pair, can cause a substantial asymmetry in the tunneling behavior at temperatures below the critical temperature, ultimately enabling the identification of the island's size by combining measurements from different temperatures and the relevant tunneling times. In contrast to traditional multi-view capture methods, our approach relies solely on a single camera capture, making it suitable for applications involving autonomous vehicles, robots, and drones. By leveraging the model's pre-trained image and video fine-tuning capabilities, we achieve reliable performance even in the absence of human annotation. Through a comprehensive evaluation, we demonstrate the DiffDreamer's superiority over existing eternals view methods, while also examining its robustness against varying latency and evaluating its performance in autonomous vehicle key frames selection for decision making purposes. Additionally, we outline a range of potential applications for this technology. The source code and models will be publicly available.

separable convolution with stride greater than 1 for downsampling, DCNNs
employ dilated convolution in this task. However, in many cases, especially
MIMO, DCNNs struggle to respond due to insufficient data in training.
Additionally, the dilated convolution's ability to sample non-standard
gridpoints comes with a drawback: the feature maps' size becomes impractical
for feature exchange among different layers, which hampers the model's
performance. Consequently, current research often combines multiple dilated
convolution kernels, resulting in patchy features that complicate feature
exchange. In this study, we introduce the $E$-net, an innovative network
structure that facilitates effective feature exchange through a proposed
feature aggregation block, allowing the extraction of diverse yet meaningful
features. We also investigate the performance of the proposed $E$-net in MIMO
frameworks through three applications: general classification, semantic
segmentation, and object detection, demonstrating its efficacy in extracting
important features, even with k>2. Moreover, its feature aggregation block

Due to the inherent stiffness of robotic systems, which limits their work area, artifical stiffness must be introduced through position feedback and control. This study presents a novel method for enhancing the end effector's regulatory precision of an open-loop robotic system, specifically focusing on the J2 Rethink Robotics robot. An end effector spatial model is first proposed, followed by an analysis of its stochastic movement and identification of a threshold for stability. This stability threshold is utilized to adjust an online PID controller's parameters dynamically, ultimately improving upon existing solutions like Sequential Least Squares. An experimental assessment of this regulatory method was conducted using the J2 robot's actual data, which showed that it outperforms Current-Shunt estimation by nearly doubling the system's stability. This research demonstrates a versatile approach that can be easily adapted to other robotic systems with similar characteristics. To analyze numerous event types in the context of time-to-event data, we develop MSE, an innovative method utilizing multi-state life course models. These models consider diverse states and their transitions to quantify the probability and duration of events in a timeline framework. For simultaneous processing of multiple event types, we leverage a myocardial infarction dataset from the Paris cohort of the Three-City Study, focusing on the occurrence and sequence of cardiovascular events. Using this information, MSE assesses the predictive accuracy of models via cross-validation and grounds its selection of states and transitions through stochastic Bayesian methods. Consequently, MSE produces individualized predictions and estimates the population's overall burden and timeline of events. Additionally, MSE analyzes the conditional probability of events given previous experiences and reveals event patterns, gender differences, and how exposure to one event influences other events. Notably, MSE identifies distinct patterns in women's health, emphasizing the broader implications of this method for analyzing timelines of events, including multiple state models in epidemiological studies and clinical trials. The MSE implementation is now available on the R package'msa'.

Despite century-old theories, solving the Schrödinger equation for large molecules remains a highly challenging task due to the necessity of achieving accurate results at multiple length scales. We introduce the molecular continuum model (MCM), which partitions a molecule into atomic nuclei and an electron gas separated by an energy barrier. We demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the coupled ordinary differential equations that govern the system's evolution under the Born-Oppenheimer and time-dependent density matrix approximations. We also develop a quadrature approach that utilizes scaled Gaussian weights and abscissas to approximate solutions at nuclei locations, proven to converge to the exact solution. We show that by adjusting variables and energy factors, the MCM reduces to the well-established Pöschl-Teller model at optimal points, enabling the calculation of bound state solutions with high accuracy. We test the MCM approach using quadrature-based implementations that solve the Tully model, a simplified version of the molecular continuum model, and demonstrate its applicability and accuracy in modeling large test molecules by comparing its results with other methods. We also explore the versatility of the MCM framework by adapting it to account for electron-phonon coupling in peptides and to simulate the interaction between a quantum dot and carbon nanotubes. Our findings indicate that the MCM offers a versatile and efficient approach to modeling molecules with high accuracy in both theoretical and practical applications. We also assess the computational scalability of these methods and analyze their time and space complexity. The effectiveness of deep neural networks depends largely on high-quality labels, 
especially when training to eliminate noisy data generated through the same 
neural networks. Methods like using multiple classifiers to filter out noise 
and self-correction techniques have shown some promise, yet they are often limited 
in their applicability and computationally costly. We introduce an innovative 
mechanism, the Bayesian Label Restoration Mechanism (BLRM), designed to counter 
label noise by leveraging the predictive uncertainties provided by Bayesian 
models. In experimental comparisons with existing noise-filtering methods, BLMR 
consistently yields superior performance and demonstrates significant potential 
for real-world medical image categorization tasks. Labeled data corrected using 
BLRM can translate to improved performance in subsequent tasks with fewer images, 
reducing the need for large datasets or costly annotations. What's more, our model 
is adaptable for use in other areas by simply fine-tuning BLMR with new datasets, 
transferring it to apply to other domains with minimal additional processing. 
Ultimately, the benefits of using BLMR include reduced data annotation costs and 
the ability to transfer it to other domains with minimal additional processing.

This research aims to numerically model and experimentally validate the concept of anomalous shielding, a phenomenon occurring in granular materials where electromagnetic fields are suppressed when they undergo thermal treatment or mechanical stress. Our study delves into the realm of identifying hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali text, a task that has seen increasing attention worldwide but remains underexplored for Indian languages. We've compiled a large dataset rich in hate-speech examples, along with detailed annotations that outline the severity of each post. Our analysis examines the underexposed HIBI task, comparing the effectiveness of various neural network architectures and loss functions to improve performance. We also investigate the effectiveness of transfer learning, showcasing for the first time, results achieved by neural networks in identifying hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali languages. Our findings highlight that underexplored domains can benefit from transfer learning, particularly when trained on annotated data from related tasks. We also recommend the utilization of multi-loss functions to tackle the underannotation issue in the HIBI dataset. Ultimately, this study contributes to the understanding of identifying hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali languages, paving the way for related NLP tasks such as sentiment analysis and text generation, and promoting the use of annotated datasets to develop more accurate machine learning models. In this research, we investigate the Korovkin theorems for two groups of operators, 
${\mathcal L}_1({\mathcal P})$ and ${\mathcal L}_2({\mathcal P})$. The first group includes operators like $H_j[\cdot]$ that represent partial summations of the Fourier series of a function, as well as nonlinear operators like $\Pi_1[\cdot]$ that approximate functions by trigonometric polynomials up to the $j$-th degree, under certain convexity and monotonicity constraints. Our results in this part generalize the findings of Rassias. The second group involves operators like $T_I[\cdot]$ that apply a linear combination of linear operators, as well as operators like $S_j[\cdot]$ that apply a linear combination of modulated linear operators, under certain constraints on the modulating coefficients. Our results for ${\mathcal L}_2({\mathcal P})$ generalize the findings of the second part of the theorem. The key to our proof lies in accurately estimating the norms of the differences between ${\mathcal L}_2({\mathcal P}})$ operators and the corresponding linear operators in various function spaces. Our research, despite some minor errors in the original proof, corrects and generalizes a paper by P. P. Korovkin. We further apply our results to investigate the almost everywhere convergence of the nonlinear operators. We develop a new class of operators that combine properties from both groups. We utilize our findings to prove a new Korovkin theorem for this new class of operators. We further generalize this result to the category of probabilistic operators. We demonstrate that in many instances, the nonlinear operators converge to the identity operator in a stronger norm than their linear counterparts. We utilize our results to investigate the convergence of nonlinear operators in the spaces $C_{\rm b}(X)$, ${\mathcal M}_{\rm b}(X)$, and ${\mathcal S}_{\rm b}(X)$ for various metric spaces $X$. In the case of $C_{\rm b}(X)$, our results, in a simplified form, generalize a paper by P. P. Korovkin. We further utilize our results to investigate the convergence of nonlinear operators in various function spaces, such as ${\mathcal M}({\mathcal P}})$, $C({\mathcal P}})$, and ${\mathcal S}({\mathcal P}})$.

Let G be a graph of order n and size r. In 2001, Li and Chen introduced the concept of Hamiltonian density, defining it as r times the largest integer less than or equal to n divided by r. They then posed a question regarding graphs with this specific density: must all such graphs contain a Hamiltonian cycle? In 2016, Chen and Li explored another quantity, independence density, by examining the largest integer less than or equal to n divided by the size of the largest independent set in G. They questioned whether all graphs with this specific density contain an independent set in G. In 2020, Han and Li expanded upon these concepts by defining pancyclic density as r times the largest integer less than or equal to n divided by 2, and asked whether all graphs with this specific density contain a Hamiltonian cycle. In this study, we examine these three densities and solve Li and Chen's problem, demonstrate that there are graphs with a specific density that contain a Hamiltonian cycle but no pancyclic paths. We further solve another of Han and Li's problems, proving that there are graphs with a specific density that contain a Hamiltonian cycle but no k-longest cycles with a specific diameter. We also provide a solution to part of Li and Chen's independence density problem, confirming that all graphs with the specified density contain an independent set in G. We identify whether all graphs with the specified diameter contain such an independent set in G. Finally, we prove that all graphs with the specified pancyclic density contain a pancyclic path. We express our results through the notation and terminology commonly used in Chinese publications.

Global crises like the COVID-19 pandemic transform how people move throughout a city, inducing significant changes in daily commuting patterns. To grasp how economic disparities were affected by the pandemic, a study focused on capturing the spatial behavior of people in major cities like New York City and London through the analysis of publicly available data on subway systems. By examining the movement patterns in 2020 when compared to historical controls, it was discovered that people with higher incomes tended to maintain their routine more effectively but overall, the pandemic led to a decline in inter-personal interactions among people of varying socioeconomic statuses, particularly affecting the lower socioeconomic class who saw their interactions diminish at a greater rate. This study's findings indicate that the pandemic brought forward a shift in urban interactions that was initially expected to occur years into the future as a result of income inequality. The study's data and methods are openly available to inform future research on the effects of global crises on human behavior in the context of urban spaces. The study's key contributions involve the quantitative assessment of how economic disparities were exacerbated during the pandemic, the impact of which will likely have lasting effects on urban planning. Two field-separating methods are tested: a conventional approach based on the two-phase material's characteristic lengths and an innovative mechanism-related approach. We assess the efficacy of these techniques using computational fluid dynamics simulations of two- and three-dimensional flows through uneven media and find that both methods effectively surpass the current standard, known as the volume-averaged technique. Through our investigations, the innovative approach emerges as the superior choice due to its capacity for analytical assessment and its capacity for performance optimization in intricate settings, achieving up to 2.4 times faster results with comparable accuracy to the other methods. We validate our findings by analyzing them using a cost-effectiveness metric that takes into account the interplay between the computational cost and benefits associated with the proposed approach. We conclude our investigations by identifying areas for further improvement and potential applications for the proposed method in a wide range of contexts, including the analysis of two-phase flows. This framework established that any matter inside a star must adhere to the conditions defined by Penrose's causal hood, with key implications for the development of gravitational waves as they emerge from the surface of the star. The metric used in Novikov and Penrose's paper relates to Schwarzschild's solution of the Einstein equations when no matter is present. In this research, we explore idealized gas models with a constant pressure schedule, effectively creating a warp travel metric according to the conditions set by Novikov and Penrose. However, it becomes clear that these solutions cannot be linked to a non-singular, in extend, matter distribution. In response, we also examine a modified version of Einstein's gravity with a negative constant present, and in this altered context, we find that there are new solutions which are consistent with Novikov and Penrose's conditions. In a technical note, related to this research, it is demonstrated that a previous solution, examined by Aliev and Eroglu with a different pressure schedule, does not in fact satisfy Novikov and Penrose's conditions as claimed. The number of smart grids and cities is increasing rapidly, driven by developments in advanced infrastructure management technologies. However, implementing new metropolitan information systems often poses significant technical challenges, particularly when trying to integrate diverse, heterogeneous data sets into a unified framework. To address these issues, this research introduces GUIDES, a proof-of-concept framework that focuses on linking geospatial data within smart city grids. GUIDES combines a range of extensions to the GeoSPARQL protocol for managing geodata, incorporating query functions, data visualization, and machine learning techniques. By leveraging flexible data structures and layering mechanisms, GUIDES facilitates the implementation of new features and applications on top of a standardized platform. To demonstrate its efficacy, this paper introduces a test case based on the city of Aachen, Germany, and showcases its capabilities through a web-based demonstration. By providing a scalable and flexible platform, GUIDES serves as an adaptable foundation for developing innovative smart city projects. Guidelines for integrating new features are also offered to facilitate replication and integration into other smart city initiatives. A live demonstration of the GUIDES test case can be accessed via the website guides-citydata.org. TERS is an emerging technique that offers unparalleled insight into the electronic and geometric properties of nanomaterials. This method relies on the interaction between a near field microscope and nanostructured scatterers to reveal the underlying chemistry and electromagnetic properties of materials at the nanoscale. Current explanations for TERS images and spectra rely on approximate models, including the framework provided by equations by Gonzales and Novak, as well as other simplifications. These models divide the influence of electromagnetic phenomena into two parts: non-radiative processes that excite and probe the material, and radiative processes that transmit energy through radiation, often considered separately. In contrast, we present a comprehensive quantum mechanical model capable of isolating the distinct roles of these phenomena and show that their effects can be separated in some cases. This model also highlights situations in which these phenomena are intertwined, for example, when analyzing attenuation patterns. The methodology employed used to derive this quantum mechanical model involved first describing the emission of electrons and radiation as a result of their interlinked processes, and then applying the principles of rapid scanning to relate the resulting radiation to the material's properties through probe-material interactions, and ultimately describing this relationship using probe-material interactions with a focus on property mappings. Utilizing this approach, we have revisited the interpretation of NAP and RGE, and demonstrated their application in determining materials' properties at their underlying geometric and chemical basis. It is anticipated that this quantum mechanical model, in conjunction with an accompanying computer software, will play a significant role in the continued development of NAP and RGE experiments, in understanding the underlying phenomena associated with these methods, and in explaining the results obtained from these experiments. This software, shared publicly at www.github.com/UofA-Nano/feldQuantum, enables users to differentiate between electromagnetic and chemical influences on materials' properties, and to explore a broad range of applications including detection of spin polarization, study of low dimensional materials, investigation of nonlinear effects, analysis of systems having multiple probes and targets, assessment of phase and charge transport, evaluation of materials' stability through probing, estimation of materials' properties at higher energy scales, and many others. This unique behavior occurs at a nearly identical temperature of 238 K where both ferroelectricity and the Néel temperature coalesce. Despite being a molecular ferroelectric, this temperature transition isn't a result of 1/2 O3-like antiferroelectricity, instead it's attributed to a significant change in entropy, however the underlying source of this high entropy is unclear. Through the use of high-resolution solution nuclear magnetic resonance, we found that the Néel temperature is accompanied by a substantial molecular motional phenomenon. Furthermore, the high entropy is also supported by the observation of large low-frequency vibrational modes, the flexibility of the sulfate ion, and the discovery of an entropic contribution from the amplification of low-spin states of the ammonium ion. High-performance training of distributed deep neural network models depends on accurate gradient propagation, but network I/O limitations can impede this process, leading to inaccurate gradient estimates that worsen as training progresses. Existing solutions often overlook the underlying physics of communication delays, instead striving for faster network transmission. To address this issue, we investigated the source problem by examining how gradient propagation decays due to communication delays. We found that due to stochastic gradient descent, gradient decay primarily affects the gradient's magnitude rather than its direction. Based on this insight, we employed Bayesian principles to reconstruct the full gradient vector, considering communication delays as an additional source of noise. Through theoretical analysis and numerical validation, we established that our iterative solution attenuates gradient direction errors, thus enhancing model training accuracy, despite the presence of communication delays. Numerical simulations confirmed that our approach can effectively mitigate assessment error and enhance model convergence, even under extreme communication limitations. We validated these results through real-world testing using the MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 datasets. Furthermore, we employed numerical propagation methods to mitigate communication delays, rather than a parameter estimation approach, and demonstrated that any efficient propagation scheme can be adapted for a Bayesian reconstruction. We also explored the generalizability of our approach by assessing its performance on image classification models with larger reconstruction biases. Our proposed method significantly improves the performance of distributed deep neural network training, making it more suitable for performance optimization. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first comprehensive analysis of accurate gradient propagation in the literature. As a result, our approach has been successfully applied to performance optimization for distributed training, and its implications could be extended to other related optimization problems. The empirical results and numerical data used in this research are publicly available at https://github.com/huoyuan-li/SEMIBR. An implementation of the SEMIBR framework is publicly available at https://github.com/huoyuan-li/SEMIBR. Our findings imply that accurate gradient propagation is crucial to model performance, and thus, should be addressed by network optimization. We also discovered that disregarding communication delays, which continually worsen model performance, is not a viable strategy. To address these issues, we employed Bayesian principles to reconstruct the full gradient vector, and through theoretical analysis and numerical validation, we established a general approach to mitigate these issues. Our proposed method has been successfully applied to performance optimization for distributed performance and is extendable to other related problems. Our work demonstrates that accurate gradient propagation is crucial to model performance, and thus, should be addressed by network optimization.

The goal of multi-robot systems is often to execute complex tasks that are beyond the capabilities of individual robots. To achieve these tasks efficiently and safely, it's necessary for the robots to cooperate with each other in a coordinated manner. However, for robots to work well together, they need to operate within predictable environments. If these expectations change due to internal or external factors, the robots' behavior must adapt quickly to maintain task efficiency. We propose a novel approach to small-scale robotic task force management, which allows for a seamless transition from internal to external goal changes. By incorporating a predictive model of robot behavior, the task assignment is handled through a distributed optimization method, which ensures that goal changes are implemented with minimal disruption. We evaluated the performance of this approach on a robotic swarm that executes a complex navigation task around obstacles. Compared to a static task allocation framework, our approach demonstrated adaptability and efficient collision avoidance when faced with changing robotic agent preferences. By simulating these changing preferences, we showed that our approach outperformed other methods, achieving up to 25% better results. These findings highlight the effectiveness of our framework in managing task assignment for robust, autonomous task execution. Ultimately, our work has implications for the development of more agile and adaptable robotic swarms by taking into account the dynamic interplay between internal and external goal changes. For tasks like route-finding and map-learning, robots often benefit from using maps at various scales. In this paper, we develop a single data structure called Hierarchical Topological Map (HiTMap) that captures information about a space at different levels, from its layout to its local features. To improve navigation and learning in unfamiliar settings, HiTMap represents two levels of a map: a large-scale diagram with its local details integrated into smaller topographic illustrations. Unlike other mapping techniques, HiTMap uses a two-part representation that simplifies data collection and learning. We demonstrate how HiTMap facilitates learning and route-finding in unfamiliar environments, using a simulated robot navigating through two diverse spaces. Furthermore, we highlight the advantages of using a two-part map representation in tackling these tasks. Our results show that by learning from diagrams with integrated local information, a robot can achieve better results in following a mapped route compared to learning from individual data points. Additionally, a robot trained on navigating with HiTMap's diagrams is more efficient in finding new routes between two unknown locations than one using a learned probability distribution. This study focuses on creating interactive tools for analyzing complex time-based data, which are displayed using various techniques such as heatmaps, time series, and scatterplots. We aim to develop interactive tools for analyzing two-dimensional, one-dimensional, and multidimensional time-based data that enhance understanding, memory, and engagement, which are key objectives of human-computer interaction. We also examine the use of these interactive tools in enhancing screen engagement and explore their potential in other fields, such as medicine and sports. This study demonstrates that interactive visualizations involving multidimensional time-based data can be challenging but still enhance engagement and understanding, which are key principles of human-computer interaction. We also identify opportunities for further research on these interactive tools and their potential applications in various fields. Through a controlled experiment, we examined the effectiveness of interactive tools in enhancing engagement, understanding, and memory, which are key objectives of human-computer interaction. We analyzed three interactive tools for analyzing two-dimensional, one-dimensional, and multidimensional time-based data. We found that the interactive tools for two-dimensional and one-dimensional data were easy to understand and provided accurate summaries when used for analysis. However, the interactive tool for analyzing multidimensional data was more challenging to understand, as it was difficult to see the connection between the different dimensions without additional support. To overcome this challenge, we analyzed three strategies for enhancing the understanding of these interactive tools by adding support for analyzing trends across different dimensions through spatial visualizations. We conducted a controlled experiment to compare the effectiveness of these interactive tools in enhancing engagement, understanding, and memory in three different applications, including medicine, sports, and finance. We analyzed the engagement and understanding of users when using the interactive tool for analyzing two-dimensional, one-dimensional, and multidimensional time-based data with and without additional support for analyzing trends across different dimensions. We found that the interactive tool for analyzing two-dimensional and one-dimensional data was easy to understand and provided accurate summaries when used for analysis. However, the interactive tool for analyzing multidimensional data with additional support for analyzing trends across different dimensions was more engaging, as users were able to provide summaries for all dimensions, which enhanced their understanding and memory, which are key objectives of human-computer interaction. The implementation of Electronic Health Records has exponentially increased access to health information, yet collecting such data poses significant challenges regarding data privacy, confidentiality, and consistency. Leveraging EHR data for machine learning advancements has proven difficult due to the diverse structure, variability in attributes, and scarcity of samples of the same modality. In an attempt to overcome these obstacles, a novel graph neural network called the Diverse Similarity Graph Neural Network is being presented for multi-entity extraction and relationship identification in EHRs. By representing entities as nodes in a graph where nodes are associated based on similarity and links are applicable, the Diverse similarity Graph Neural Network uses a combination of heuristic methods and graph neural networks to determine node similarities and scan the graph topology, where a specialized attention mechanism is applied to aggregate information from nodes' local neighborhoods and linearly combine outputs from various models, thus achieving state-of-the-art performance in entity extraction and relationship identification and ultimately contributing to improving data privacy by minimizing the collection of sensitive information without compromising effectiveness. Diverse similarity Graph Neural Network demonstrates exceptional performance on multi-entity extraction and relationship identification tasks within various synthetic and real-world datasets, resulting in results superior to those of leading models like BERT and ELMo, specifically reducing error rates, improving precision rates, and achieving a perfect score in some cases. In particular, for the final run on Med-BERT, our method achieved a linear combination of models that surpasses the performance of Med-BERT, resulting in a relative decrease in error rates of approximately 14.00%, 23.85%, and 41.67%, and a relative increase in precision rates of about 0.29%, 0.23%, and 0.34% respectively, while also obtaining a perfect score in some cases. The source code for the Diverse similarity Graph Neural Network is available for download on GitHub at https://github.com/azoest/DSGNN. We model the soft surface as a time-independent potential and derive an expression for the surface charge density in terms of the applied potential, temperature, and dynamic properties of the electrolyte. Through numerical calculations, we investigate the effect of solvent polarization on the electric double layer, revealing a more pronounced depletion zone near the soft surface, with a higher degree of solvent polarization increasing the width of this depletion zone. Additionally, we find that solvent polarization influences the surface charge density and electrolyte concentration at the interface, shifting to higher or lower values depending on the polarization condition and electrolyte concentration. We also consider how solvent polarization affects the screening length within the electric double layer, observing a minimum in the screening length at a specific electrolyte concentration due to a change in the configuration of the ions in the presence of solvent polarization. Overall, our results demonstrate the significance of solvent polarization in understanding the behavior of the electric double layer at the interface of a soft surface. The theoretical findings are substantiated by experimental data from a study on a charged graphene surface, showing a correlation between the Zeta potential and electrolyte concentration due to solvent polarization. A relay can significantly lower energy consumption in wireless networks by re-routing data, yet optimizing overall energy efficiency involves deciding when, how, and by which relay to utilize. To address this, a novel method for network encoding is introduced, combining information transmission and energy efficiency into a single optimization process. Encoding decisions are taken simultaneously with other critical tasks such as power distribution and relay scheduling, resulting in an intricate problem. By transforming this into a mixed-integer linear optimization problem, an off-the-shelf algorithm can be used for near-optimal solutions.
